It tells me whose hours enter the price and whose refusal stops the wages.","severity":"major","category":"voice"},{"text":"8. Major, borderline, premise. What Guardian is buying is never made plain. Davies says "Guardian purchases calculations," but the returned table "did not agree with Guardian's independent calculation," so Guardian computed the table itself anyway; and in XI Halden says "Guardian paid us to stop that table leaving," which is a third thing (a checking service). A reader who is asked to care about "What had the customer purchased?" for twelve chapters may reasonably not know. One line would settle it (Davies bought the machine table to release his own computers, and recomputed the ages above forty-six as his check; or Guardian bought a second, independent computation and compared the whole). I mark it borderline because the book's ambiguity may be intentional; if so, the last chapter should let Charles or Henry name it.","quote":"Guardian purchases calculations,","severity":"major","category":"borderline, premise"},{"text":"9. Minor, chronology. Ch. II. "Eleven years earlier" and "He read it on the fifteenth of August" are the only anchors, and no year is given for the opening or for II. The first absolute date in the book is "October 1847" in VII. A reader can back the year out of "the test packet from 1851" and "three years before" in I, but should not have to. Say "August 1843" once; it also announces the point of departure to readers who know the real date.","quote":"Eleven years earlier","severity":"minor","category":"chronology"},{"text":"10. Minor, unexplained term. Ch. I. "Mr Neale had the Lothbury packet." Nothing tells the reader this is another customer's job (it is named again as "the Lothbury packet" three paragraphs later). "Another office's packet" or the customer's name would do.","quote":"Mr Neale had the Lothbury packet.","severity":"minor","category":"unexplained term"},{"text":"11. Minor, logic. Ch. XI. "Halden's reply to Guardian contained the source sheet, the preparation copy, the cards, both run traces, the delivery ledger ..." An office would not post its whole delivery ledger, with other customers' entries, to one customer. "An extract from the delivery ledger" or "the ledger page."","quote":"Halden's reply to Guardian contained the source sheet, the preparation copy, the cards, both run traces, the delivery ledger ...","severity":"minor","category":"logic"},{"text":"12. Minor, typography of embedded documents. Halden's marginal authorization ("Second comparison to follow. Delivery permitted to preserve date." / "E. H."), the public sentence in VIII, the qualification in IX, and both inventory headings in XII run as ordinary body paragraphs, while *deputy, if required*, *mechanism trace exact*, *pressure of business*, and *I authorized delivery before the independent comparison was complete* are italic. Choose one treatment for quoted documents (block or italic) and apply it throughout. In the same pass: the paragraph in VIII ends "could all be named." and "Only then did Davies permit the prospective packet to close." begins on a new line without a paragraph break, and several sentences in IX, X, and XI run far past the file's wrap width ("He held the office pen ...", "In April Lovelace returned ...", "The additional wages ...", "She read Halden's answer again ...", "too softly; Neale had already begun ..."), which suggests later edits pasted in.","quote":"Second comparison to follow. Delivery permitted to preserve date.","severity":"minor","category":"typography of embedded documents"},{"text":"13. Minor, clarity. Ch. II. "Any later proposal must answer it before anyone is asked to build a metaphor." The line is the chapter's best joke and the reader cannot be sure what the metaphor is (the Engine as it exists "most completely in his mind"?). One more beat earlier in the exchange would earn it.","quote":"Any later proposal must answer it before anyone is asked to build a metaphor.","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"14. Minor, redundancy. Ch. III tells the discovery of the reversal three times: "For the first week Halden tried to bound the Engine ... That failed."; "He discovered the reversal after covering the largest drawing with unpaid accounts ... began with the answer instead."; "The Notes supplied the route." The second is the scene; the first and third can be folded into it.","quote":"For the first week Halden tried to bound the Engine ... That failed.","severity":"minor","category":"redundancy"},{"text":"15. Minor, unexplained term. Ch. III. "Halden crossed out an automatic return that required machinery he could not price." "Automatic return" (the cards backing to repeat a sequence) is not explained, and it is the one exclusion that matters most to what the apparatus cannot do. Half a sentence.","quote":"Halden crossed out an automatic return that required machinery he could not price.","severity":"minor","category":"unexplained term"},{"text":"16. Minor, clarity. Ch. III. "It was more than Babbage expected and less than Halden could afford to waste." Why a wealthy man would expect less than twenty-five pounds for four weeks is not clear; if the point is that Babbage expected the possibility of refusal to be cheap, say so.","quote":"It was more than Babbage expected and less than Halden could afford to waste.","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"17. Minor, clarity. Ch. IV. "Davies closed the Notes upon his finger." then, next paragraph, "Davies turned the pages. He paused at the exclusions". Two consecutive paragraphs open with "Davies"; the second does not say which document's pages (the proposal, evidently, since he then "closed the proposal"). "Davies turned the pages of the proposal."","quote":"Davies closed the Notes upon his finger.","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"18. Minor, clarity. Ch. IV. "The second refusal arrived from Manchester in a wooden box." Nothing before it has been called a refusal; Davies's scene ended on "the first condition on which they agreed." If Davies's refusal to hold an opinion is the first refusal, say it once, because the pairing is a good one.","quote":"The second refusal arrived from Manchester in a wooden box.","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"19. Minor, accounting. Ch. V. "The capital page named three thousand pounds. Babbage supplied half. Outside subscribers supplied one thousand through the trust. Guardian's feasibility and test payments supplied four hundred. Halden supplied one hundred." The sums add (1,500 + 1,000 + 400 + 100), but Guardian's payments are receipts for services, not capital, and a book this exact about accounts should not let Halden call them capital. "The page of funds" or "sources of money" instead of "capital page."","quote":"The capital page named three thousand pounds. Babbage supplied half. Outside subscribers supplied one thousand through the trust. Guardian's feasibility and test payments supplied four hundred. Halden supplied one hundred.","severity":"minor","category":"accounting"},{"text":"20. Minor, antecedent. Ch. VI. "Then leave the finding so. I won't have him condemn a sound shaft to make this week's account easier." "Him" is Babbage, who has not yet entered; on first reading it attaches to Halden, who has just spoken. Name him.","quote":"Then leave the finding so. I won't have him condemn a sound shaft to make this week's account easier.","severity":"minor","category":"antecedent"},{"text":"21. Minor, plausibility. Ch. I: "Every few seconds the card reader lifted, admitted a stiff rectangle, and let it fall." Ch. VIII: "The first attempt consumed the morning" for five and a fraction cases of thirty cards each, and twelve cases take an afternoon. At a card every few seconds, 360 cards is under an hour; the hours must be going to reading back, manual entry, and transcription between cases, which is exactly the book's point, but VIII never says so. One sentence in VIII crediting the day to the human steps would turn a wobble into a theme.","quote":"Every few seconds the card reader lifted, admitted a stiff rectangle, and let it fall.","severity":"minor","category":"plausibility"},{"text":"22. Minor, chronology. Ch. VIII. "That prohibition had taken nearly seven years to earn." From August 1843 to a test in spring 1851 is closer to eight; from the compact (unstated, presumably early 1844) it is a little over seven. "Seven years" or "more than seven years."","quote":"That prohibition had taken nearly seven years to earn.","severity":"minor","category":"chronology"},{"text":"23. Minor, ambiguity. Ch. VIII. "Neale signed both preparation checks." In a book that turns on two hands for two signatures, this reads on first pass as one man signing both checks, which is the failure of Chapter I. If it means the preparation check for each of the two runs, say "the preparation check for each run."","quote":"Neale signed both preparation checks.","severity":"minor","category":"ambiguity"},{"text":"24. Minor, phrasing. Ch. IX. "Thomas Neale was retained for ten hours a week, which made the theoretical quarter larger." The clause is doing arithmetic the sentence does not show (130 hours against the 80 promised). Give the number or cut the clause.","quote":"Thomas Neale was retained for ten hours a week, which made the theoretical quarter larger.","severity":"minor","category":"phrasing"},{"text":"25. Minor, clarity. Ch. IX. "Halden had advertised for another checker. None could yet challenge a prepared deck without Neale's supervision". "None" implies applicants who came and failed; if no one came, say so; if some came, one clause on them would show the market for the skill.","quote":"Halden had advertised for another checker. None could yet challenge a prepared deck without Neale's supervision","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"26. Minor, abstraction. Ch. IX. "For a moment, the old alliance between conditions and limits reappeared." The narrator naming his own theme. Cut; the exchange it follows ("Is in no contract and no account.") already shows it.","quote":"For a moment, the old alliance between conditions and limits reappeared.","severity":"minor","category":"abstraction"},{"text":"27. Minor, arithmetic left to the reader. Ch. IX. "At forty hours per verified packet, the office could deliver two." Four packets due in one quarter is 160 hours against 80, the entire objection, and no one says "one hundred and sixty." Neale's "I have eighty hours, sir" is close; let Lovelace or Neale say the other number once.","quote":"At forty hours per verified packet, the office could deliver two.","severity":"minor","category":"arithmetic left to the reader"},{"text":"28. Minor, continuity (soft). Ch. IX has Neale "retained for ten hours a week" and "Neale's paid hours for that day were over"; Ch. XI has him copying under voice for four days, "By the third evening Neale's voice had roughened." Two years have passed and his retention may have grown, but the book does not say so, and it is the book that taught the reader to count his hours. One phrase in X or XI.","quote":"retained for ten hours a week","severity":"minor","category":"continuity (soft)"},{"text":"29. Minor, terminology drift. Ch. X. "the edge of Guardian's source sheet slipped from beneath the roll." In I and XI "the Guardian source sheet" means the signed return that does not arrive until 1 April 1854; in August 1852 the office has "specimen or provisional figures." Since "It does not read Guardian's source sheet" is the chapter's last word, make it "Guardian's specimen sheet" or the copied 1851 source, whichever is meant.","quote":"the edge of Guardian's source sheet slipped from beneath the roll.","severity":"minor","category":"terminology drift"},{"text":"30. Minor, antecedent. Ch. X. "She drew the successor register from beneath the roll and closed it over his letter." No letter of Babbage's has been placed on the bed in the scene; "his letter" is the answer she read pages earlier. "over his written answer" or put the letter on the bed when the roll is opened.","quote":"She drew the successor register from beneath the roll and closed it over his letter.","severity":"minor","category":"antecedent"},{"text":"31. Minor, clarity. Ch. X. "He did not consent or refuse. He recommended that the office wait. Halden adopted the recommendation". Consent to what is not clear at this point: her unfinished table, the paid training plan, or the request "to accept no work beyond Neale's demonstrated reach." Name it.","quote":"He did not consent or refuse. He recommended that the office wait. Halden adopted the recommendation","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"32. Minor, clarity. Ch. XI. "When Halden began to call the third rescue, she put one finger beneath the first." The construction (call the third [column] a rescue) has to be reverse-engineered from the sorting sentence before it. "When Halden began to call the third column a rescue."","quote":"When Halden began to call the third rescue, she put one finger beneath the first.","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"33. Minor, clarity. Ch. XI. "Before you send another circular," implies an earlier circular; none has been sent (Babbage's improvement notice in VII was not circulated). "Before you send a circular."","quote":"Before you send another circular,","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"34. Minor, attribution. Ch. XI. "Neale lowered his wooden case to the floor. / 'Is there something wrong?' Halden asked. / 'Could you put the order in, sir?'" The last line is Wills's, but the paragraph before it is Neale's action, so the reader assigns it to Neale until "'Not the copying,' Wills said." This is the emotional peak of the Wills thread; attribute it.","quote":"Neale lowered his wooden case to the floor. / 'Is there something wrong?' Halden asked. / 'Could you put the order in, sir?'","severity":"minor","category":"attribution"},{"text":"35. Minor, phrasing. Ch. XII. "found the returned table among his father's successful papers." "Successful papers" is either a slip for "successor papers" (the successor register is in the packet) or an irony the sentence cannot carry. If irony, "among the papers of his father's successes"; if slip, fix.","quote":"found the returned table among his father's successful papers.","severity":"minor","category":"phrasing"},{"text":"36. Minor, plausibility. Ch. XII. "the close hand Henry knew from the Notes." The Notes were printed; a hand is known from manuscript. "from her letters among his father's papers" or "from the manuscript of the Notes."","quote":"the close hand Henry knew from the Notes.","severity":"minor","category":"plausibility"},{"text":"37. Minor, terminology. Ch. XII. "her unanswered succession question." The phrase appears here for the first time; the object is the unfinished three-column table from X ("competence, paid time, authority to refuse"). Either use "succession" in X or describe the table in XII.","quote":"her unanswered succession question.","severity":"minor","category":"terminology"},{"text":"38. Minor, clarity. Ch. XII. "Not that sheet. The alteration is on the next." through "'Yes,' Charles said. 'You see.'" The reader cannot tell what drawing they are following or why the line passing "beneath another sheet" matters (an improvement never finished, presumably). A phrase of Henry's perception would carry it.","quote":"Not that sheet. The alteration is on the next.","severity":"minor","category":"clarity"},{"text":"39. Minor, spelling consistency. The manuscript mixes American and British forms: "labor" (II), "honor" (IV), "favored" (V), "recognized" against "theatre" (III), "initialled," "pencilled," "grey-edged," and both "toward" and "towards" throughout. Pick one convention; British suits the setting and the "Mr" without a stop.","quote":"recognized","severity":"minor","category":"spelling consistency"},{"text":"40. Minor, tic. Negation as narration is used often enough to become a mannerism: "He did not call for Babbage. He did not yet call for the clerk"; "No one declared success."; "No one altered the figure."; "No one remarked upon the change."; "He removed none of the papers."; "Neither man looked towards the office door."; "He did not consent or refuse." Each is fine alone; together they announce the author's hand. Keep the best three.","quote":"He did not call for Babbage. He did not yet call for the clerk","severity":"minor","category":"tic"},{"text":"41. Minor, tic. The finger on the line is the book's governing gesture, and it is used past the point of return: "She put one fingernail beneath the wages due."; "She set one finger on it."; "She left one finger where the two paths had inherited the same value."; "she put one finger beneath the first."; "Lovelace's finger reached the final operation and stayed there"; "He touched the prepared copy."; "his blank strip arrested beneath the first line." Reserve it for Neale's strip and Wills's ruler, where it means something, and let the others use their hands differently.","quote":"She put one fingernail beneath the wages due.","severity":"minor","category":"tic"},{"text":"42. Minor, slack passages. The back half of IV (the Whitworth box and Lovelace's two columns, all in summary) and the first page of IX (capacity arithmetic in the narrator's voice) are the two places a reader will skim. Both would take a line of speech or an object.","severity":"minor","category":"slack passages"},{"text":"43. Note. The title phrase never appears in the text, and its referent is open: Lovelace's ruled volume, the sixteen-page compact with its stopping clauses, or the whole packet. That may be intended; if not, one use in V or XII would fix it.","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"44. Note, real world. Guardian Assurance's own office was in Lothbury (11 Lothbury, I am fairly but not fully sure). Calling another customer's job "the Lothbury packet" will trip readers who know that.","quote":"the Lothbury packet","severity":"note","category":"real world"},{"text":"45. Note, real world. "The paper had arrived after the Notes." Lovelace's proposal was written on 14 August 1843 while the Notes were in final proof; publication in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs was, I believe, September 1843 (fairly sure). "After the Notes were finished" is exact; "after the Notes" is arguable. Not an error for an alternate history, but this is the sentence that sits on the point of departure.","quote":"The paper had arrived after the Notes.","severity":"note","category":"real world"},{"text":"46. Note, real world. The historical Lovelace was in London and gravely ill through August 1852; the Ockham pencil scene in X near the end of that month is a softening of her condition. The book's rule ("could work for an hour and lose the afternoon to it") makes it internally consistent, and the departure is allowed; I record it because a reader who knows will feel it.","quote":"could work for an hour and lose the afternoon to it","severity":"note","category":"real world"},{"text":"47. Note, real world. Chapter XII's "several autumn afternoons" of 1871 sit inside a short window: Babbage died on 18 October 1871 (confident). The scene works as an inventory made because he is dying, and the text half says so ("his father tired before they could finish an argument"), but a phrase acknowledging how little time is left would stop the reader checking. I believe Henry was in England that autumn; not certain.","quote":"several autumn afternoons","severity":"note","category":"real world"},{"text":"48. Note, character. Babbage does not change inside the 1843–1855 story; his last line to Halden is "That preserves the account by surrendering the work." The concession arrives sixteen years later, in the coda. This is a defensible design (the tragedy of a fixed man), and XII earns it; but the reader should know it is chosen. If the author wants any movement earlier, VI already has the seed ("Enter both").","quote":"That preserves the account by surrendering the work.","severity":"note","category":"character"},{"text":"49. Note, character. Lovelace is right in every dispute in the book. Her one flaw, refusing her own deputy and so making the venture's judgment depend on one person, is present and well placed ("It depends upon my continuing to insist that he is single"; "I would not have let you"), but it is left for the reader to connect to her accusation against Halden. One more beat, from William or from her, would make her a person rather than a conscience.","quote":"It depends upon my continuing to insist that he is single","severity":"note","category":"character"},{"text":"50. Note. "In 1900, Henry opened the packet again." Nothing motivates the year. A reason (an inquiry, a move, his own work on the mill) would cost a sentence and make the coda feel less like an author choosing a round number.","quote":"In 1900, Henry opened the packet again.","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"51. Note. Chapter I is dense with terms the reader cannot yet decode (clause eleven, configuration register, successor register, run trace, "sold four dates with hands for two," the 1851 packet, the qualification on capacity). On reread it is the best chapter; on first read the last page is cryptic. That is a fair trade, but the author should know the first-time reader finishes I on faith.","quote":"sold four dates with hands for two,","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"52. Note. Halden forgetting his own waiver until he opens the ledger ("He remembered the morning") is psychologically framed by the book ("The third course had felt least like a decision"), and it is the point. Some readers will still not believe that the man of accounts forgot the largest job's exception within weeks. Dramatizing the Friday (finding 6) would remove the need for him to forget.","quote":"He remembered the morning","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"53. Note. "Babbage answered too quickly." (VIII) and "Charles answered too quickly." (XII) are an echo, and a good one. Keep it; make sure nothing else in the book uses the phrase.","quote":"Babbage answered too quickly.","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"54. Note. The aphoristic paragraph-closer is the book's signature ("Monday had filled itself before it arrived."; "A reasonable wrong answer recruited the reader."; "Since the government's withdrawal, no one had offered him a refusal that did not also end the undertaking."). Most earn their place; the density in II, III, and V means some land as manner rather than meaning. Consider cutting a fifth of them.","quote":"Monday had filled itself before it arrived.","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"55. Note. "Lovelace came to his rooms in Dorset Street." Babbage owned the house at 1 Dorset Street; "rooms" suggests lodgings. "His house" is plainer and true.","quote":"Lovelace came to his rooms in Dorset Street.","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"56. Note. "For several seconds, only the fire answered." is the one stock sentence in an otherwise unstock book.","quote":"For several seconds, only the fire answered.","severity":"note","category":"general"},{"text":"57. Note. The novel Margaret reads aloud in VII (the drowned brother, the estate) is never named, and the scene is better for it. Leave it.","severity":"note","category":"general"}]}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-review/v1","kind":"review","text":"# Voice comparison: The Book of Conditions

*Method: I read Version 1 (V1) in full, then Version 2 (V2) in full, and only then compared them, using a line diff of those two files alone. No other file was opened. Real-world confidence is given in square brackets where it matters. The two are the same novella in the same twelve chapters: every scene, figure, date and stage direction matches, and the narration is identical except for five sentences that V2 adds. V1 is about 300 words longer (12,715 against 12,418), spread over 26 hunks in the diff. Everything else that differs is in what characters say aloud.*

## 1. Verdict

**Version 1 is the better book: by a clear margin on character voice, by a modest margin as a whole book.** The whole difference lies in the spoken lines of Babbage, Lovelace and Halden, mostly in Chs. I-VI and IX-XI. In V1 those three sound like three people. Babbage is a grand, grudge-bearing anecdotist who argues from his own record ("I have not forgiven it the economy"; "I learned that from Clement, who kept the tools and called it the custom of his trade"; "It is an engine as a keyhole is a house"). Lovelace is a dry mathematician-wit who thinks in functions ("none of us can be solved alone"; "a very beautiful clock that nobody is obliged to consult"). Halden is a plain tradesman who talks in weights, edges and contractions ("I can't price a thing without an edge"). In V2 the same speeches have been pared into one shared register: contraction-free, balanced, aphoristic, the narrator's own. The opposition that drives the book (Babbage's rhetorical generality against Halden's and Lovelace's insistence on a bounded claim) survives as position but no longer as speech. V1 also plants what V2 leaves bare. Clement is explained. "The store, the mill" in Ch. III prepares the mill of Ch. XII. The "Upper House" aside in Ch. I is paid off as "both Houses" in Ch. XI. The loom of Lovelace's own Notes surfaces in Ch. X. V1 also gives the last chapter something to contract against: old Charles's "But they bought the table" lands harder after a Babbage who has talked so freely. Counting every difference I could find (33, listed in section 3), V1 is better at 25 (17 clearly, 8 slightly), V2 at 4 (all slight), and 4 are even. V1's costs are real but small: two garbled lines ("I have been said more about all my life"; "whatever its register chooses to call them"), one weakened antecedent, one stray spelling. V2 has no error of its own, but it removes more than it repairs.

**Narrator: a tie.** The narration is the book's strongest asset and is shared. V2's five extra sentences are three good ones ("Knowing did not make the risk smaller."; the Davies sentence; "knowledge that purchased coal"), one neutral, and one slightly redundant (the Ch. XII sentence pre-states the book's last image). **Character voices: V1, clearly.** Confidence: high, roughly 85-90%, that V1 has the better voices, and roughly 80% that a careful reader would call it the better book overall. The doubt is taste. A reader who prizes the book's own austerity, or who weighs V1's two slips heavily, could prefer V2's leaner speeches. I do not think that preference survives a side-by-side reading of Chs. II and III, where V2's principals become interchangeable.

## 2. The voices, person by person

### Babbage

**V1.** He argues from his own record and grievances and ends long sentences on a barb. "The Treasury answered me in fewer words. I have not forgiven it the economy." (II) "I did not know it in 1834, I do not know it this morning, and I shall not know it on the day your committee requires me to swear to it." (II) "It is an engine as a keyhole is a house." (III) "I disliked that transfer from the first drawing, and I have the drawing to prove it." (VI) "I have argued that for twenty years, and I did not expect to argue it in this room." (IX)
- *Distinct?* Yes. He is the only speaker who reaches for history, anecdote and simile.
- *Right for who and when?* Very. The grievances are exact (the Treasury's 1842 refusal; Clement keeping the tooling as "the custom of his trade" [~85%]). "The store, the mill" are his own terms [certain]. The two "wrong figures" asides (I and XI) are his best-known anecdote, from *Passages from the Life of a Philosopher* [~95%].
- *Forced?* The keyhole and loaves similes arrive a little on schedule, with a modern comic timing. One line is muddled (V, "whatever its register chooses to call them").
- *Arc.* From voluble (1843-52) to old Charles's "Not there." and "But they bought the table." (XII). The arc is the more moving for the distance travelled.

**V2.** The same positions in the shared register. "You have defined the apparatus by subtracting every power that makes the architecture general." (III) "The Engine carried what it was given." (I)
- *Distinct?* Only by position. In Ch. III he and Halden speak the same kind of sentence ("One of those orders can be priced without being mistaken for the whole." / "I need its limits before I can begin.").
- *Right?* Acceptable but generic. The wit, the anecdote and the self-regard are mostly gone. "Clement" is named twice (II, III) and never explained, and "the mill" first appears in the last chapter.
- *Forced?* Nothing. The 1843-to-1871 arc is flatter because there is less to lose.

### Lovelace

**V1.** Cool, exact and teasing. She thinks in mathematical figures, answers with counter-questions, and uses her own Notes as authority. "...each becomes a function of the other two, and none of us can be solved alone." (II) "Without it you have a very beautiful clock that nobody is obliged to consult." (IV) "You charge us for refusing risk, Mr Halden, and then you buy some yourself. I should like to know which of you to believe." (V) "If it had, I should go home and leave you both to it." (IX) "...as the loom weaves flowers..." (X)
- *Distinct?* Yes. She is shorter and lighter than Babbage, and more formal and more playful than Halden.
- *Right?* Good. "Function" and "solved" are period-correct mathematical usage. The loom and the music are lifted from her real Note A [~90%]. "I should like" suits an earl's wife. The real Ada's letters are more exuberant and rhetorical than this cool Ada [~75%]. Both versions choose restraint, but V1 at least gives her wit and one real image. Her late spareness ("It is good." "It does not read Guardian's sheet." "I would not have let you.", X) is more affecting against a witty earlier self.
- *Forced?* "I have been said more about all my life." (III) is ungrammatical. "None of us can be solved alone" is a shade precious but in character.

**V2.** The same skeleton in legal diction. "...each may be made answerable to the others." (II) "You charge for refusing risk and then purchase some yourself." (V) "It might carry them to a passage no composer had set down note by note." (X)
- *Distinct?* Less. Her speech now sounds like Halden's "paper". The wit and the mathematician survive only in lines both versions share ("cast a metaphor in brass"; "Our surprise would not be its intention.").
- *Right?* Not wrong, just less herself. No slips.

### Halden

**V1.** A plain-spoken tradesman: contractions, concrete nouns (weights, edges, bills, wages), short declaratives, and a habit of turning any principle into an account. "I can't put practicability on a bill, sir. The man who pays it will want to know what it weighs." (III) "I can't price a thing without an edge." (III) "If I didn't, I'd be paid for delay and you for hope." (V) "She's told me which repair I can order and still call it a test." (VI)
- *Distinct?* Yes. He is the only principal whose diction matches his trade and the narrator's account of him (he "weighed the packet because the absurdity of eleven pounds amused him"). Twelve of his speeches in Chs. III-XI use contractions. The formal Halden of Ch. I is a man in a crisis addressing a clerk.
- *Right?* Yes. Contractions are period-plausible for a London engineer.
- *Forced?* No.

**V2.** Formal throughout the office chapters. "I cannot put practicability on a bill." (III) "Division makes no one competent." (III) "Otherwise I would be paid for delay and you for hope." (V) "Is in no contract and no account." (IX)
- *Distinct?* Weakly. These are often the better aphorisms, but they are the same kind of aphorism as Babbage's and Lovelace's, so the tradesman is lost. His only contractions are "That's the same fellow" (at home, VII) and, unprepared, two in Ch. XI ("I won't answer cancellation...", "I wasn't going to take it out.").
- *Right?* Acceptable, though "cannot" and "I would have" suit a solicitor better than an estimator.
- *Forced?* No.

### Davies

Identical in both, and the most consistently individuated principal voice in either: clipped, interrogative, an auditor's list of exclusions, dry irony. "...then I wish him every honour due to principles. Guardian purchases calculations." (IV) "Then do not call it an Engine in anything you send to my directors." (IV) "Before or after I pay?" (IV) "Read it again." (VIII). He is right for an actuary. The real Griffith Davies was, I believe, a Welsh actuary connected with the Guardian [~80%], and the book gives him no regional colour, which is defensible. The only difference is narratorial. V2's added sentence ("An assurance office could survive eloquence only by turning it into assumptions another calculator could inspect.") states what his lines already show. It is a good sentence, not needed, not harmful.

### Narrator

Shared, and the book's strongest asset: cool, exact, ironic, moving between heads. Latinate abstraction is broken by a concrete image, and the book is fond of the reversed expectation ("An absurd answer accused itself. A reasonable wrong answer recruited the reader."; "The mechanism's resistance entered Farrow's life first as Friday."; "Monday had filled itself before it arrived."). Its habits (the compressed antithesis, the closing pronouncement, "not X but Y") also shape the principals' dialogue. That is why paring the dialogue (V2) makes everyone converge on the narrator. It sometimes names what a gesture has already shown ("He was overtaken by a joy so close to relief that for several seconds he could not distinguish them."), and it turns abstract in the exposition of Chs. IX and XI. V2's five additional sentences are: three good (II "Knowing did not make the risk smaller."; IV the Davies sentence; VII "knowledge that purchased coal"), one neutral (II "The laughter did not settle anything, but it altered what could be said next."), and one slightly redundant (XII). A wash.

### Other voices (identical in both)

These are the book's most alive voices, and the model for what the principals could be. Neale is teacherly and exact ("A strange figure stops you. Watch the one you expect.", IX). Wills is deferential and careful ("I read the copy back, sir.", I; "The one before, Mr Neale.", XI; "Could you put the order in, sir?", XI). Farrow is blunt and moral ("I won't have Mr Babbage condemn a sound shaft to make this week's account easier.", VI). The foreman speaks like a deposition ("Nothing by itself. Coupled, the drive takes up before one turn. I can show the load.", VI). Margaret is practical ("Is this sum in the bank on Friday?", VII). William has few words ("You promised me one hour." "You promised both.", X). Henry and old Charles (XII) are terse. One quibble: Wills, Neale and Henry never use a contraction ("I cannot read that one."), so they are as formal as the principals. Clerks of the 1850s would probably have said "can't".

## 3. Where they differ and which is better at each place

Numbered in chapter order. "V1 only" or "V2 only" means the other version has no equivalent text.

**Ch. I**

1. *Babbage on the trace.* V1: "The first value supplied for forty-seven, and nowhere after it. Every transfer that follows is true. ... The Engine carried, as it was built to carry, precisely what it was given." V2: "The first value supplied for forty-seven. After that, every transfer is true. ... The Engine carried what it was given." **Even.** V1 is more Babbage ("observe where", the flourish). V2 is clearer ("nowhere after it" needs a second look) and hits harder.
2. *Babbage's aside (V1 only).* "I have met that confusion before, Mr Halden, in a member of the Upper House. I had not expected to meet it here." **V1.** It is his own famous anecdote (the MP who asked whether right answers come out of wrong figures [~95%]). It shows him striking first, gives Halden's flat "Of course it is." something to deflate, and is paid off in Ch. XI. Cost: the antecedent of "Of course it is." drifts (see 4.A3).

**Ch. II**

3. *Narrator on Lovelace (V2 only).* "Knowing did not make the risk smaller." **V2, slightly.** A good short beat after a long sentence. It gives her a moment of exposure the dialogue never will.
4. *Babbage on the Treasury.* V1: "The Treasury answered me in fewer words. I have not forgiven it the economy." V2: ends at "...called it an answer to the Engine," he said. **V1.** The pun on economy (words and money) and the grudge are exactly Babbage. V2's accusation is fine but characterless.
5. *Babbage on committees.* V1: "I have sat on committees, Lady Lovelace. I have not seen the clauses improve them." V2: "You suppose that because the government would not continue, a committee of private persons may be made wiser by clauses." (end of speech) **V1.** Dry and personal, and the title is correct for a countess.
6. *Lovelace on interdependence.* V1: "...then each becomes a function of the other two, and none of us can be solved alone." V2: "...each may be made answerable to the others." **V1.** Her mathematical idiom against Halden's clause-language.
7. *Babbage on not knowing the form (V1 only).* "I did not know it in 1834, I do not know it this morning, and I shall not know it on the day your committee requires me to swear to it." **V1.** The date is right (the Analytical Engine designs begin in 1834 [~90%]). The rhythm is his. It states the objection to constitutions more vividly than the shared line before it.
8. *Babbage on permanence.* V1: "And whatever I sign becomes permanent the moment the ink is dry. I learned that from Clement, who kept the tools and called it the custom of his trade." V2: "If I sign an inferior arrangement into permanence, you will have protected the undertaking..." **V1.** It is historically exact, and it explains the "Clement" the narrator has just named. V2 leaves the name bare.
9. *Lovelace on the purse.* V1: "I have been perfectly explicit about that." V2: "That omission is not disguised in the paper." **V1, slightly.** Closer to speech and to her briskness. V2's is neat but written.
10. *After "He laughed despite himself." (V2 only).* "The laughter did not settle anything, but it altered what could be said next." **V1, slightly.** The bare line and the paragraph break are crisper. The addition explains a beat that already reads.

**Ch. III**

11. *The pricing exchange.* V1: Halden, "I can't put practicability on a bill, sir. The man who pays it will want to know what it weighs." Babbage, "...the store, the mill, the reading of the cards, the printing, and so down. One of those orders might be priced, I suppose, without anyone mistaking it for the whole, though I have seldom met the man who would not." Halden, "Tell me where it stops. I can't price a thing without an edge." V2: "I cannot put practicability on a bill." / "One of those orders can be priced without being mistaken for the whole." / "I need its limits before I can begin." **V1.** This is the clearest case in the book. V1 gives two speakers two dictions (concrete nouns and contractions against a long sentence with a barb) and echoes the narrator's "Halden weighed the packet". In V2 both men say the same kind of sentence.
12. *Halden on division.* V1: "It doesn't make anybody competent. It tells me whose hours go on the bill, and whose word stops the wages." V2: "Division makes no one competent. It tells me whose hours enter the price and whose refusal stops the wages." **Even.** V1 sounds like Halden. V2 is the better aphorism and picks up "division" from Babbage's line.
13. *Babbage on the exclusions.* V1: "...every power that makes the architecture worth defining. It is an engine as a keyhole is a house." / "I've defined what another man can be asked to finish." V2: "...every power that makes the architecture general." / "I have defined what another person may be asked to finish." **V1.** The keyhole line is the best insult in the book. V2's "general" is flat.
14. *Lovelace's aside.* V1: "People will say more. I have been said more about all my life." V2: "People will say more." **V2, slightly, as printed.** V1's idea (she has been over-described all her life) is right and echoes Ch. II, but the sentence is ungrammatical. Fixed, V1 would win.

**Ch. IV**

15. *Narrator on Davies (V2 only).* "An assurance office could survive eloquence only by turning it into assumptions another calculator could inspect." **V2, slightly.** It names what his lines already do, and "calculator" is used in its period sense of a person.
16. *Lovelace on the second column (V1 only).* "Without it you have a very beautiful clock that nobody is obliged to consult." **V1.** The best line V1 adds for her: wit, and it gives the second column a reason the reader can feel.

**Ch. V**

17. *Halden on cost.* V1: "they both cost money." V2: "both require money." **V1, slightly.** "Cost" is exact and plain. "Require" is off (see 4.B1).
18. *Babbage on "successor".* V1: "You make the Engine sound like this instrument's grandson. ... they do not descend from a box of six registers, whatever its register chooses to call them." V2: "The later arrangements belong to the Engine; they do not descend from this instrument." **V1, slightly.** "Grandson" is a fine reversal of the relation. The tail is muddled (see 4.A2). With the tail cut, clearly V1.
19. *Lovelace and Halden on risk.* V1: "You charge us for refusing risk, Mr Halden, and then you buy some yourself. I should like to know which of you to believe." / "If I didn't, I'd be paid for delay and you for hope." V2: "You charge for refusing risk and then purchase some yourself." / "Otherwise I would be paid for delay and you for hope." **V1.** Her formal teasing against his plain retort. In V2 both are parallel compressions.
20. *Halden's last line.* V1: "That's why it gets its own signature." V2: "That is why it receives its own signature." **V1, slightly.** Same register argument.

**Ch. VI**

21. *Babbage at the works.* V1: "I disliked that transfer from the first drawing, and I have the drawing to prove it. The failure proves those alterations necessary." V2: "The failure proves those alterations necessary." **V1.** It pays off the narrator's "a transfer he had disliked from the beginning" and exposes the vanity inside "proves".
22. *Halden on correcting the drive.* V1: "I'd have Farrow correct the drive we paid him to make. Your way may be better. It isn't this machine yet." V2: "I would have Farrow correct the shared drive we paid him to make. Your proposal may be better. It is not yet this machine." **V1, slightly.** Blunter and more personal. V2 is more precise ("shared drive").
23. *Halden on Lovelace's ruling.* V1: "She's told me which repair I can order and still call it a test." V2: "She has told me which repair this test permits me to order." **V1.** "Still call it a test" is the book's theme in a tradesman's mouth.

**Ch. VII**

24. *Halden on the subscriptions.* V1: "Then I book their money against machinery we haven't promised and can't price," V2: "Then I enter their subscriptions against machinery we have not promised and cannot yet price," **Even.** V1 is more spoken. V2 echoes the book's "enter" motif.
25. *Narrator on Margaret (V2 only).* "That winter, knowledge without a public title was still knowledge that purchased coal." **V2, slightly.** A sharp social point in one sentence, consistent with the book's concern for uncredited work. V1's paragraph ends more crisply, but V2's line adds something.

**Ch. IX**

26. *Babbage on the hours (V1 only).* "...as though hours were loaves ... The railways built themselves on exactly that principle, and nobody asks them to apologise." **V1.** It is period-apt (calls on shares, as in Ch. VII) and characteristic. The irony of citing the railways after 1847 is Babbage's blind spot, not the author's.
27. *Babbage at the door.* V1: "...fixed for ever, like the tides. ... I have argued that for twenty years, and I did not expect to argue it in this room." V2: "...is itself fixed." **V1.** The twenty years is right (*Economy of Machinery*, 1832 [~90%]), and the sentence shows a man surprised by his own audience.
28. *Lovelace's reply (V1 only).* "If it had, I should go home and leave you both to it." **V1.** Dry, and it seeds the withdrawal the next chapters enact.
29. *Halden's interruption.* V1: "Isn't in any contract or any account." V2: "Is in no contract and no account." **Even.** V1 is more idiomatic. V2 is more clipped.

**Ch. X**

30. *Lovelace on music.* V1: "...that it might weave them, as the loom weaves flowers, into a passage no composer had set down note by note." V2: "It might carry them to a passage no composer had set down note by note." **V1.** V1 recalls her real Note A ("weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves", and the music passage [~90%]). V2's "carry them to a passage" is generic.

**Ch. XI**

31. *Babbage on what people will say (V1 only).* "I have twice been asked, by members of both Houses, whether the machine gives right answers when it is given wrong figures. They will not need to ask again. They will think they know." **V1.** It matches Ch. I and the real anecdote, and it is a strong, bitter turn.
32. *Halden's question.* V1: "On what statement?" V2: "Upon what statement?" **V1, slightly.** Consistent with his speech everywhere else.

**Ch. XII**

33. *Narrator on the tape (V2 only).* "Each time, proof and failure returned beneath one fastening." **V1, slightly.** The book's last sentence ties the faded tape round all three papers, and V2 has said it once already.

**Tally:** V1 clearly better at 17 (2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 13, 16, 19, 21, 23, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31); V1 slightly better at 8 (9, 10, 17, 18, 20, 22, 32, 33); even at 4 (1, 12, 24, 29); V2 slightly better at 4 (3, 14, 15, 25). All four V2 wins are small, and three are narrator sentences.

## 4. Errors and confusions

Legend. **Error**: a plain mistake of fact, grammar or logic. **Major**: a slip that damages a scene or the book's credibility. **Minor**: a small slip, inconsistency or unclear phrase. **Note**: not a fault as such; a usage or period point a careful reader might notice, or an uncertainty. I found no Major problem in either version. Each version's full list is 4.S (shared) plus its own items.

### 4.S Present in both versions (identical text)

- **S1. Ch. III, Minor.** "Babbage looked at the sheet as if Halden had covered a portrait during a funeral." Covering portraits is a mourning custom, not an affront, so the simile points the wrong way or is too oblique to read.
- **S2. Ch. IV, Minor.** "answers could be produced by experienced human computers". This is a retronym. In the 1840s-50s "computers" alone meant people who calculated, as at the Nautical Almanac Office [~80%]. "Human" is a modern disambiguation.
- **S3. Ch. VII, Minor.** "The credit shock, she wrote, did not alter what the current subscribers had been shown." "Shock" in this economic sense is 20th-century [~85%]. Period wording would be "the crisis", "the panic" or "the pressure in the money market". The event itself (October 1847) is right.
- **S4. Chs. IV, VII, VIII, IX, Note.** Modern method and management vocabulary in narration and speech: "The protocol must still tell us whether the difference entered with your source..."; "Halden held the configuration register and the stopping rule"; "frozen configuration"; "prospective packet"; "eighty independent checker-hours"; "His coordination fee"; "card reader"; "run trace". If the modernity is the alternate-history conceit (a Victorian world that invents test discipline early) it is a strength. Nothing marks it as deliberate, though, and it sits beside true period usage, so S2 and S3 read as accidents.
- **S5. Chs. IX and X, Minor.** "At forty hours per verified packet, the office could deliver two." and "Four packets at forty hours make a hundred and sixty" (IX), against "Lothbury's and Guardian's were the two small packets, a week of Neale's hours apiece." (X). A week of Neale's hours is ten ("ten hours a week", IX), not forty. The plot's causal arithmetic rests on these figures, so the drift should be explained or removed.
- **S6. Ch. XI, Minor.** "The remaining obligations took the rest of the year to close. On the last day of March 1855..." From April 1854 the rest of the year is nine months; the closure takes twelve.
- **S7. Chs. I, IX, X, Note.** "Return" carries three senses: the customer's annual return ("release signed returns no earlier than 1 April"; "Guardian's signed return arrived"), the table sent back ("the returned table"), and "the third return arrived with a query". A moment's confusion in X.
- **S8. Ch. IX, Note.** Elliptical exchange: "'Then we stage the work.' 'I know.' She reached for the capacity sheet. 'I mean the final comparison. When would Neale do it?'" The turn (staging solves preparation, not the independent comparison) has to be reconstructed. The comparably oblique Ch. XI exchange ("Only the other part as well.") pays off within a few lines.
- **S9. Ch. III, Note.** The thirty-day term is never closed on the page. Halden asks for "four weeks" on day 26, and Babbage "paid the fee that evening from his own purse, four days inside his term. No refusal was written." The reader must assume that paying ends the term.
- **S10. Ch. II, Note (not an error).** A deliberate departure. Lovelace's real proposal to take charge of Babbage's affairs dates from mid-August 1843 (a letter of 14 August [~80%]), and he did not accept it. Here he accepts thirty days. The dates given (the 15th, the 18th) fit. Everything else before the departure that I can check is right: the Notes and Menabrea's Turin material, Dorset Street, Ockham, 1834, the Treasury's 1842 refusal, Clement, Griffith Davies's assurance connection and Babbage's 1826 work on assurance, Whitworth of Manchester, the October 1847 crisis, Great Cumberland Place and 27 November 1852, Guardian in Lombard Street [~75%], 7 April 1854 being a Friday (computed), Babbage's death in 1871.
- **S11. Voice, Note.** Wills, Neale and Henry speak without a single contraction ("I cannot read that one."). Only Farrow, Margaret and Edward at home (and, in V1, Halden) use them. See section 2.

### 4.1 Version 1: S1-S11 apply, plus

- **A1. Ch. III, Error (small).** "People will say more. I have been said more about all my life." It is ungrammatical: "said more about" cannot take "I" as subject. The sense is "more has been said about me". The idea is good (it echoes Ch. II's list of labels Lovelace has been given). A repair would be "I have had more said about me all my life."
- **A2. Ch. V, Minor.** "...they do not descend from a box of six registers, whatever its register chooses to call them." "Register" is used for the mechanical registers and for the ledger-like "successor register" in one sentence. "Its" has no clear antecedent, and "chooses to call them" (what?) is undefined. The "grandson" sentence before it is excellent; cut the tail.
- **A3. Ch. I, Minor.** "I have met that confusion before, Mr Halden, in a member of the Upper House. I had not expected to meet it here." / "Of course it is." Halden's reply now sits behind two new sentences, and its antecedent ("a human failure") is three sentences back. The nearest "it" is "that confusion", which makes no sense.
- **A4. Ch. IX, Note.** "nobody asks them to apologise" is the only -ise/-ize inconsistency in either text (elsewhere: authorized, recognized, dramatize, mechanized, with British -our/-re). As history the claim is arguable after the 1847-49 railway collapse, which the book's own Ch. VII crisis makes ironic. It is acceptable as Babbage's blind spot.
- **A5. Ch. XI, Note.** "They will not need to ask again. They will think they know." It is accurate to the real anecdote but opaque unless the reader knows it. The "answer" they will think they have is that the machine gives wrong answers.

### 4.2 Version 2: S1-S11 apply, plus

- **B1. Ch. V, Minor.** "In an account," Halden replied, "both require money." An architectural necessity and a discretionary enlargement cost money; they do not "require" it. V1's "they both cost money" is exact.
- **B2. Chs. II, III, XII, Minor.** Under-planted names. "He had made much the same argument against Clement and against the Treasury." (II) and "the old Clement network" (III) leave Clement unexplained. "Underneath lay a drawing of the mill" (XII) is the first mention of the mill. That is fine for a reader who knows Babbage and a gap for anyone else.
- **B3. Chs. III-XI, Note.** Halden has no contractions in the office until Ch. XI ("I won't answer cancellation with a paragraph about the Engine.", "I wasn't going to take it out."), and nothing prepares them. A deliberate loosening under pressure is possible, but the same register is not established for the other speakers.
- **B4. Ch. XII, Note.** "Each time, proof and failure returned beneath one fastening." It pre-states the final image.
- **B5. Ch. II, Note.** "The laughter did not settle anything, but it altered what could be said next." It explains a beat that reads clearly without it.

## 5. What still most needs work

In V1, the better version:

1. **Carry the front-half voice work through Chs. VII-XI, and let the voices change under pressure.** In V1 the three principals differ richly in II-VI and IX. In VIII, X and XI they speak one procedural language ("Inspection of the source is not an improvement to the machine." / "...the answer will have changed the question by which we meant to judge it."; "You have used the stopping clauses as though dissolution were a completed stage." / "The wages are paid."). The crisis chapters are where each idiom should show its cost: Babbage's wit and vanity failing at the twelfth case; Halden's plainness under shame (his decisive "Release them," in X is one short line); Lovelace's mathematical figures in her illness. Give Davies his last word in his own voice. His cancellation is summarized ("Davies accepted the trace and rejected the table.") rather than heard, although he is the most distinct voice in the book.
2. **Ration the narrator's summary and pronouncement, and let more of the world in.** Keep the great sentences ("Monday had filled itself before it arrived.") but cut the ones that repeat a gesture (the "joy so close to relief" sentence in VIII; V2's "Each time, proof and failure..." is a model of a sentence to leave out). Turn the most abstract stretches into scene or object: Ch. IX's capacity paragraphs ("Thomas Neale would not leave an assurance post...", "The proposed tables were due between April and June 1854...") and the closure resolution in XI. The concrete scenes (Neale's strip, Wills's ruler, Margaret's ledger) are the best in the book. The 1854 chapters say nothing of the war declared that March [~95%], and Babbage's real hatred of street noise [~90%] would give his voice a period particular.
3. **Repair and de-modernize.** Fix V1's own slips: III ("I have had more said about me all my life."), V (cut the "register" tail), I ("Of course it is a human failure."), IX ("apologize"), and the III "portrait during a funeral" simile. Then audit the modern lexicon of S2-S4 ("human computers", "credit shock", "protocol", "checker-hours", "coordination fee", "stopping rule", "card reader"). Replace the accidental ones. For the rest, decide whether they are a deliberate alternate-history idiom, and if so let one character notice it. Consider giving Wills and Neale contractions (S11).

Cheap synthesis: V1 with those repairs, plus three of V2's narrator sentences (II "Knowing did not make the risk smaller.", IV the Davies sentence, VII "knowledge that purchased coal"), is better than either version as it stands.

An architectural necessity and a discretionary enlargement cost money; they do not "require" it. V1's "they both cost money" is exact.","severity":"minor","category":"version-2"},{"text":"B3: Halden has no contractions in the office until Ch. XI ("I won't answer cancellation with a paragraph about the Engine.", "I wasn't going to take it out."), and nothing prepares them. A deliberate loosening under pressure is possible, but the same register is not established for the other speakers.","severity":"note","category":"version-2"},{"text":"B4: "Each time, proof and failure returned beneath one fastening." It pre-states the final image.","severity":"note","category":"version-2"},{"text":"B5: "The laughter did not settle anything, but it altered what could be said next." It explains a beat that reads clearly without it.","severity":"note","category":"version-2"}]}}
