{"schema":"meaning-model-review/v1","kind":"review","text":"# Comparison: The Book of Conditions

Method: I read Version 1 in full, then Version 2 in full, before comparing anything. Afterwards I ran a paragraph-level diff so that no difference was missed. I have not tried to say which text is the revision; every judgment below is about the reading experience. Line numbers are those of the .md files (V1 / V2). Process note: at the very end, after the report was finished and checked, I ran a directory listing of this folder by mistake, which showed the names, sizes and times of other files here; I opened none of them, and nothing in this report was written or changed because of that listing.

## 1. Verdict

**Version 1 is the better book, by a clear margin** (more than modest, less than large).

The two texts are close kin. Ninety-nine percent of V2's words (spelling normalized) occur, in order, in V1, so V2 is almost V1 with cuts and a handful of local rewrites (V1 is about 12,300 words, V2 about 11,700; Chapters IX and X account for about 530 of the roughly 640-word gap, with smaller differences in III, VIII and XII). What V1 has and V2 lacks is almost entirely setup and payoff, not decoration: the thirty-day bargain closed ("No refusal was written."); the calculation office's founding and Lovelace's question "And who may refuse the manager?"; her qualification with its three written directions, of which Halden obeys one, defers one and breaks one; and, biggest of all, a dramatized 7 April 1854 at the end of Chapter X in which Halden writes the waiver into the ledger with her qualification on the shelf and Wills watching. That scene closes the ring opened by the book's first sentence, and it gives Wills's request in Chapter XI ("Could you put the order in, sir?") and Chapter XII's "final lines still widening" something to point back to. In V2 those later moments arrive without their setup, Chapter X ends on a routine image of Neale's strip, and the book never watches the decision it is built around. V2 also carries small slips that V1 does not (a tense mismatch in Ch. V, "None could yet challenge" with no antecedent, "the third rescue", "another circular" when none has been sent), mixes American and British spelling, and drops the italics that set the book's recurring documents apart.

V2's own contributions are few and small: "He did not consent or refuse. He recommended that the office wait." (Ch. X), "For several seconds, only the fire answered." (Ch. XII), the clearer "capital page" (Ch. V), and a smoother sentence in Chapter II. They are worth keeping, but they do not offset the loss of the payoffs. Confidence: high on direction (roughly nine in ten), moderate on size. The honest counter-argument is a taste for restraint: Chapter I already narrates the decision, so an editor could defend V2's quiet Chapter X ending and its tighter Chapter IX. I do not hold that view, because the cuts remove things the later chapters lean on rather than slack; but it is why I say "clear" and not "large".

## 2. Where they differ and which is better at each place

Larger passages carry line numbers. Toss-up means I could argue either way. Entries marked [KEY] are the ones that change the book.

**Chapter I**

1. Davies's letter (l.21). V1: "Guardian's own calculation, by hand, of the ages from forty-seven onward". V2: "Guardian's independent calculation from age forty-seven onward". Better: toss-up. V1 adds "by hand" (person against machine; the customer's own check is what catches the error); V2 is smoother and puts the book's key word, "independent", into the first letter.

2. Babbage at the trace (l.52). V1: "The first value supplied for forty-seven." V2: "The first supplied value." Better: V1, slightly. It says where the error lives before Halden finds 3,742 against 3,472.

3. The morning (l.115). V1: "He had not forgotten the morning." and "Neale had been checking the Lothbury office's table". V2: "He remembered the morning." and "Neale had been checking another table". Better: V1, slightly. The negative form carries Halden's avoidance, and the named client connects to Wills's "Mr Neale had the Lothbury packet" earlier in the chapter. V2 names Lothbury a paragraph later, so only texture is lost.

**Chapter II**

4. Anchoring (l.167-179 / l.164-176). V1: "Eleven years earlier, in August 1843, Charles Babbage received" ... "The paper had arrived when the Notes were finished, the Turin account turned inside out and enlarged" ... "Lovelace came to his house in Dorset Street". V2: "Eleven years earlier, Charles Babbage received" ... "The paper had arrived after the Notes, after the Turin account had been turned inside out and enlarged" ... "Lovelace came to his rooms in Dorset Street". Better: V1. The date ties the flashback to the real August 1843 exchange between Ada and Babbage (the Notes certainly appeared in 1843; I am about 75% sure of the proposal episode), and "house" is right: Babbage was a householder at 1 Dorset Street (I am confident). The word "rooms" suggests lodgings. V2's middle sentence is smoother than V1's absolute construction; that one line is worth borrowing.

5. Lovelace's reply (l.209 / l.206). V1: "If it is to be paid for," she said, "it must be governed as if somebody can say what is being paid for." V2: "A machine being paid for must be governed as if somebody can say what is being paid for." Better: V1, slightly. It sounds spoken and answers Babbage's sentence directly. V2 gains a parallel with "The machine cannot be governed..." but is stiff.

6. The image (l.255 / l.252). V1: "before anyone is asked to cast a metaphor in brass". V2: "before anyone is asked to build a metaphor". Better: V1. It names the danger concretely (a guess fixed in metal); V2's is generic.

**Chapter III**

7. [KEY] The thirty days (V1 l.303, 355-356; V2 l.300). V1: "The next afternoon, the twenty-sixth of Babbage's thirty days, he met Babbage and Lovelace in Dorset Street." and later "Babbage paid the fee that evening from his own purse, four days inside his term. No refusal was written." V2: "The next afternoon he met Babbage and Lovelace in Dorset Street." and nothing further. Better: V1, clearly. It pays off the bargain that gives Chapter II its title and its central clause ("the refusal, if it comes, is written with its reason") and keeps the calendar honest. In V2 the term simply vanishes.

8. The failed boundaries (V1 l.358; V2 l.351-358). V1: "For six evenings Halden tried to bound the Engine by selecting a portion of its proposed use, and each boundary opened upon machinery whose final form remained elsewhere." V2: "For the first week Halden tried to bound the Engine by selecting a portion of its proposed use. That failed. Every portion pulled upon machinery whose final form remained elsewhere." and, in the next paragraph, "He had spent six evenings drawing smaller boundaries around the mechanism, and each boundary had opened upon something outside it." Better: V1. It says the thing once. V2 says it twice in adjacent paragraphs, and "boundaries around the mechanism" muddles what was being bounded (a portion of its use).

9. The automatic return (l.410). V1: "Halden crossed out an automatic return, the cards backing to repeat a sequence, because he could not price the machinery it required." V2: "Halden crossed out an automatic return that required machinery he could not price." Better: V1, slightly. It tells a lay reader what is being cut (and is historically right: Babbage's cards could be backed to repeat a sequence). V2 is tighter but leaves the term opaque.

**Chapter IV**

10. First refusal (V1 l.491; V2 l.486). V1: "Guardian had refused to buy an Engine. The second refusal arrived from Manchester in a wooden box." V2: "The second refusal arrived from Manchester in a wooden box." Better: V1. In V2 "second" counts a refusal that was never named.

**Chapter V**

11. Two small ones. (a) V1 (l.552): "Farrow's works would be paid to manufacture and would be entitled to reject a drawing". V2: "Farrow's works would be paid to manufacture and was entitled to reject a drawing". Better: V1; V2 has a tense/agreement slip. (b) V1 (l.616): "The page of funds named three thousand pounds." V2: "The capital page named three thousand pounds." Better: V2, slightly; "capital page" is clearer.

**Chapter VI**

12. The foreman's line (V1 l.689). V1: "I won't have Mr Babbage condemn a sound shaft". V2: "I won't have him condemn a sound shaft". Better: V1. Babbage has not yet entered the scene; in V2 "him" reaches back to a paragraph in which the nearer male antecedent is the foreman.

**Chapter VIII**

13. Length of the wait (l.896). V1: "That prohibition had taken seven years to earn." V2: "That prohibition had taken nearly seven years to earn." No verdict. On the book's own dates (the compact follows August 1843; the cases were sealed in February 1851) the interval is a little over seven years, so V2's "nearly" is, if anything, the less accurate.

14. [KEY-ish] Human time (V1 l.941-943). V1: "The first attempt consumed the morning, most of it spent by people: each value read aloud and entered by hand, each result transcribed and read back before the next case began. The apparatus itself turned for less than an hour." V2: "The first attempt consumed the morning." Better: V1. It states the book's thesis (the machine is the small part of the hours) in the scene where the reader most needs to feel it, echoes Chapter I's "For every hour of its operation, people spent several hours", and prepares the capacity crisis of Chapter IX. The figure fits the machine's stated rate ("Every few seconds").

15. V2 adds, after the chair image, "No one remarked upon the change." (l.977). V1 stops at "Lovelace's chair stood closer to the trace than it had the day before." Better: V1. The image already says it.

**Chapter IX**

16. [KEY] The office is founded (V1 l.1074-1090). V1 adds "The calculation office was constituted in January 1852, in the solicitor's room where the compact had been signed." with the capital (Babbage 650, Halden 150, 100 unspent, "made nine hundred"), the two-signature rule, and Lovelace's marginal question "And who may refuse the manager?", answered "The account", after which "She signed the article that governed published claims and left the fourth without her name." V2 goes straight from "By December the first inquiry had become four." to "By February 1852, Halden's capacity sheet allowed eighty independent checker-hours in a quarter." Better: V1, clearly. It says where the office and its two-signature rule come from, plants the book's central question and its ironic answer (the account, into which Halden later writes his own exception), explains why "Neither could sign a customer's acceptance for Halden", and supports the nine hundred pounds that Chapter XI spends (in V2 the nine hundred appears from nowhere).

17. Neale's hours (V1 l.1095-1097). V1: "Thomas Neale would not leave an assurance post that carried a pension for an office a month old. His employer spared him ten hours a week, a hundred and thirty in a quarter on paper." V2: "Thomas Neale was retained for ten hours a week, which made the theoretical quarter larger." Better: V1. Concrete, explains why the hours are scarce, does the sum. V2's "larger" leaves the reader to work out larger than what.

18. The second checker (V1 l.1168). V1: "Two men answered; neither could yet challenge a prepared deck without Neale's supervision". V2: "Halden had advertised for another checker. None could yet challenge a prepared deck without Neale's supervision". Better: V1. V2's "None" has no antecedent.

19. V2 only (l.1168): "For a moment, the old alliance between conditions and limits reappeared. Then Halden looked again at the four deposits." V1: "Halden looked again at the four deposits." Better: toss-up, leaning V1. The V2 sentence is abstract (which two parties form the "alliance"? presumably Lovelace and Halden against the "second apparatus") and glosses a beat the interruption already shows; but it does mark the moment Halden briefly sides with her before yielding to the money.

20. The overload (V1 l.1215; V2 l.1187). V1: "Four packets at forty hours make a hundred and sixty," she said. "Can you check them independently by the final dates?" V2: "Can you independently check four packets by the final dates?" she asked. Better: V1. The shortfall (160 hours against 80) is put on the page, in Lovelace's mouth.

21. [KEY] The qualification (V1 l.1260-1275; V2 l.1228-1238). V1: "It began in her usual close hand.", then the diagnosis, then "Below that the lines stood farther apart, and each direction began at the margin." and three italic lines: "Accept no fifth." / "Pay for Mr Wills's instruction in hours of its own." / "Before the first return arrives, name who checks when Mr Neale cannot." V2: the diagnosis alone, then "She signed and dated it." Better: V1, by a wide margin. The three directions are the payoff objects of the last third: the first is obeyed, the second is deferred (Ch. X), the third is the one broken on 7 April with the qualification in view on the shelf. They also set up the closing image (Ch. XII: "final lines still widening") and echo the three directions of Lovelace's October 1847 letter (Ch. VII). In V2, Chapter XII says "Its final directions stood farther apart, each beginning at the margin" about directions the reader has never seen. (One caution for V1: the directions map so exactly onto what follows that they slightly over-determine the failure. Still worth having.)

**Chapter X**

22. The succession page (V1 l.1343; V2 l.1303). V1: "Lovelace began a page on succession with three headings". V2: "Lovelace began another page with three headings". Better: V1. Chapter XII calls it "her unanswered succession question"; V2 never labels the page.

23. Which sheet (V1 l.1387-1394; V2 l.1347-1354). V1: "the edge of Guardian's specimen sheet slipped from beneath the roll" and "It does not read Guardian's sheet." V2: "the edge of Guardian's source sheet slipped from beneath the roll" and "It does not read Guardian's source sheet." Better: toss-up. V2's line states the theme plainly (the self-checking apparatus cannot read the source). V1 is consistent with Chapter IX, where in 1852 only "specimen or provisional figures" exist and the thickened-ink specimen is what Wills cannot read.

24. Babbage's answer (V1 l.1399; V2 l.1359). V1: "He answered her table with a recommendation that the office wait." V2: "He did not consent or refuse. He recommended that the office wait." Better: V2, slightly. Crisper, and it names Babbage's evasion; V1's "answered" also echoes the "answer" of the sentence before.

25. [KEY] The decision (V1 l.1425-1470; V2 ends at l.1388). After "On 1 April 1854 Guardian's signed return arrived, and the Lothbury office's with it", V1 plays a full scene: "On Friday the seventh both dates fell due." Wills brings the deck with "one mark in the checking column, his own"; Neale is visible through the glass with "perhaps six of his week's hours left"; "On the shelf above, beside the test packet, lay Lady Lovelace's qualification."; Halden writes the exception ("Second comparison to follow. Delivery permitted to preserve date.") and gives the order ("Release them," he said. "Mr Neale will compare the copy on Monday."); "Wills looked at the single mark and then at the margin."; then Monday's and Tuesday's returns eat Neale's hours "until the packet came back tied with the office's own green tape." V2 ends the chapter at "He drew the first new source beneath his strip." Better: V1, by a wide margin; the largest single difference. It dramatizes the act the whole book is built around; repeats the ledger words of Chapter I with the reader now knowing what the qualification says; lets Wills witness the order (so his silence in Chapter I and his request in Chapter XI mean something); and closes the ring with the book's first sentence. V2 has the facts (Chapter I) but never watches the choice, and its Chapter X ends on a routine image. It is also where V1 pays a small price: see A7 in Section 3.

**Chapter XI**

26. What Halden sends (V1 l.1475; V2 l.1393). V1: "the page of the delivery ledger". V2: "the delivery ledger". Better: V1, slightly. A page is what one sends; "Mine is in the ledger" still works.

27. Margaret's line (V1 l.1553-1557; V2 l.1470-1473). V1: "When Halden began to call the third column a rescue, she put one finger beneath the first." and "Before you send any circular," she had said. V2: "When Halden began to call the third rescue, she put one finger beneath the first." and "Before you send another circular," she had said. Better: V1. The phrase "the third rescue" is garbled (a word has dropped), and "another circular" implies one has gone out when Halden has only imagined it.

**Chapter XII**

28. First sentence (V1 l.1647; V2 l.1564). V1: "found the returned table filed with his father's successes". V2: "found the returned table among his father's successful papers". Better: V1, slightly. The irony is carried directly.

29. The season (V1 l.1657; V2 l.1574). V1: "several afternoons of that last autumn". V2: "several autumn afternoons". Better: V1, slightly. The words "last autumn" put Charles's death (October 1871) in the room.

30. The hand (V1 l.1670; V2 l.1587). V1: "the close hand Henry knew from her letters to his father". V2: "the close hand Henry knew from the Notes". Better: V1. One knows a hand from letters; the Notes are printed.

31. The silence (V2 l.1605). V2 adds "For several seconds, only the fire answered." before "That was Halden's question," Charles said at last. V1 has the "at last" without the pause. Better: V2. It earns the "at last".

32. The drawing (V1 l.1714; V2 l.1633). V1: "Underneath lay a drawing of the mill, its carriage crowded with pencilled corrections of several dates." V2: "Underneath lay a drawing crowded with pencilled corrections." Better: V1. Specific (the mill, its carriage) and it carries the years.

33. The last section (V1 l.1763; V2 l.1681). V1: "In 1900, deciding what should pass after him, Henry opened the packet again." V2: "In 1900, Henry opened the packet again." Better: V1, slightly. It repeats the father's inventory ("what would pass into his custody") in the son's generation.

**Whole book**

34. Spelling. V1 is uniformly British ("towards" 18 times, "honour", "labour", "favoured", "rumour", "grey", "pencilled", "initialled"). V2 mixes: "toward" 12 times beside "towards" 6, and "honor", "labor", "favored", "rumor" beside "pencilled", "initialled", "grey", "theatre". Better: V1.

35. Typography. V1 sets the ledger exception (both times), the public sentence, Lovelace's marginal question, the qualification with its directions, and Charles's inventory line in italics. V2 sets the same documents in roman and keeps italics only for phrases inside sentences ("deputy, if required"; "I authorized delivery before the independent comparison was complete."), which is inconsistent as well as weaker. Better: V1. These documents are the book's recurring objects; setting them apart lets the reader recognize them when they return.

**Trivial differences (no verdict):** Ch. II tag "she said" after "Then it should be easy to refuse" (V1 only); Ch. III "more than Babbage had expected" / "more than Babbage expected"; Ch. IV "He turned the pages of the proposal and paused" / "Davies turned the pages. He paused"; Ch. VIII "Neale signed the preparation check for each run" / "Neale signed both preparation checks"; Ch. X "He left the papers where they were" / "He removed none of the papers" and "She held the drawing flat where" / "She left one finger where"; Ch. XI tag "Wills asked." (V1 only).

**Tally.** V1 better in 29 places, V2 better in 3 (11b, 24, 31), toss-up or no verdict in 4 (1, 13, 19, 23).

**Differences that make a version worse.** In V2, relative to V1: the loss of the April scene (25), of the qualification's directions (21), of the office's founding (16), of the thirty-day payoff (7) and of the named first refusal (10); the redundant passage (8); the small slips (11a, 12, 18, 27); the spelling and italics inconsistencies (34, 35); and, mildly, the over-explaining "No one remarked upon the change" (15). In V1, relative to V2: the three directions are so exact a forecast that they slightly over-determine the failure (21); the April scene exposes an arithmetic tension in the hours (A7 below); the added articles create a second candidate for "the copy before her" (A9 below); the Chapter VIII addition states a theme the scene could imply; and the Chapter IX founding paragraph is dense with sums. None of these is serious.

## 3. Errors and confusions in each version

Marks: Error = contradiction or factual mistake; Major = story-level problem; Minor = local problem; Note = taste call. I found no item I would class as a flat Error in either version; the nearest are A8 (an arguable contradiction of Chapter V, marked Minor) and, in V2, the omission at B1 (marked Major). Items shared by both versions carry the same text in both.

### Version 1

Major: none found.

- A1 (Minor, shared). Ch. I, l.11: "What he did not know was why the packet should have returned unopened at one end and cut cleanly along the other." The book's opening hook is never explained or revisited; it is not clear what "unopened" means for a tied and sealed packet.
- A2 (Minor, shared). Ch. II, l.232-233: "Now he saw that it was simply an empty office in it." Clumsy; "it" has no clear referent.
- A3 (Minor, shared). Ch. III / V / VI, the successor register has three origins. Ch. III l.393: "Halden placed a second, thinner book beside the report", which Babbage begins writing in before the chapter ends. Ch. V l.601: "Lovelace placed an empty ruled volume on the table." Ch. VI l.762: "It was the first time he called the successor register hers." The narrator also uses "successor register" in Ch. III before Babbage objects to the word "successor" in Ch. V.
- A4 (Note, shared). Ch. VIII, l.976: "The second run tests recurrence". Here "recurrence" means repeatability, but everywhere else it is the mathematical relation ("independently known recurrence", "sealed recurrence cases").
- A5 (Minor, shared). Ch. IX, l.1257-1258: "That possibility had been feared by both men and would have allowed them to treat her absence as consent obtained by exhaustion." They fear an outcome that would have freed them; the logic can be reconstructed but reads tangled.
- A6 (Note, shared). Ch. IX. (a) l.1231: "He held the office pen." follows a paragraph naming both Babbage and Halden. (b) l.1152: "Babbage believed that the estimate described the office they had" cuts from the strip lesson in the checking room to Halden's new office with no scene break. (c) l.1118: "He had cut Wills a checking strip from a rejected card", yet the strip is thereafter Neale's ("Neale kept the strip").
- A7 (Note, V1 only; exposed by the new April scene). Ch. IX gives "At forty hours per verified packet" and "ten hours a week"; Ch. X has Neale finish Lothbury's independent check inside the week of 1-7 April with "perhaps six of his week's hours left", and Lothbury's table leaves "with both signatures". The sums close only if Lothbury is one of the packets that need fewer hours (Neale, Ch. IX: "Some will. Some will not."), which Ch. X never says. One clause would fix it.
- A8 (Minor, shared; arguable contradiction). Ch. X, l.1411-1412: "because nobody could agree who possessed the authority to alter the schedule". Ch. V l.550 allocated it: "Price, schedule, supplier obligation, and the consequences of an accepted change belonged to Halden." In V1 the Chapter IX article also gives acceptance of customer work to the manager. The dispute after her death is more plausibly about claims or publication.
- A9 (Note, V1 only). Ch. X, l.1307: "Her signature stood alone beside the claim clauses in the copy before her." Which copy? The struck "deputy, if required" line belongs to the compact (Ch. V), but V1 now also has the office articles, where she "signed the article that governed published claims" (Ch. IX).
- A10 (Minor, shared). Ch. XI, l.1482: "Guardian invoked both." Does "both" mean both clauses, or both conditions (which are mutually exclusive: a check that failed and no check at all)?
- A11 (Note, shared). Ch. XI, l.1625: "On the last day of March 1855" follows the closure resolution with no marker; roughly eleven months have passed since mid-1854.
- A12 (Minor, shared). Ch. XII, l.1688: "That was Halden's question," ... "What had the customer purchased?" No scene has Halden ask this; the nearest is "Which object am I to price?" (Ch. III). The book's climactic question is attributed, not planted.
- A13 (Note, shared). Ch. XII, l.1712-1719: "Not that sheet. The alteration is on the next." / "One farther." It is unclear which sheet Henry finally carries to his father.
- A14 (Note, shared). Diction. The word "deck" for a stack of cards (l.1169 and elsewhere; a British 1840s writer would say pack or set, and "deck" is a later, largely American and computing usage), "protocol" (Ch. IV), "prospective comparison" and "prospective packet" (Ch. VIII-IX), "checker-hours". I am fairly sure, not certain, of these usage dates. Possibly intended as fable register, but it undermines the period surface.
- A15 (Note, V1). Ch. X, l.1468: "as other exceptions had". It asserts a pattern of exceptions; Chapter XI names only two (February 1852, April 1854), and 1853 is one summary paragraph.
- A16 (Note, shared). Ch. I, l.21: "Guardian's own calculation, by hand, of the ages from forty-seven onward". If Guardian hand-computed those ages, why did it need the table? A spot-check as a term of the first commercial job would explain it, but nothing says so.

### Version 2

- B1 (Major). Ch. X ends at l.1388, "He drew the first new source beneath his strip.", before the decision the book is built around. The frame opened in Chapter I is never rejoined on the page; Wills's silence (Ch. I) and his request (Ch. XI) lack the witnessed order behind them; Chapter XI begins with the reply to Guardian and no bridge from Chapter X. (Arguable as a choice for restraint, but I hold it as story-level.)
- B2 (Minor). Ch. IX / XII. The qualification as shown has no directions ("She signed and dated it.", l.1238), yet Ch. XII says "Its final directions stood farther apart, each beginning at the margin." and ends on "its final lines still widening toward the end". The only widening-line document the reader has seen is the 1847 letter in Ch. VII.
- B3 (Minor). No founding of the office. "Halden's new office" (Ch. IX), "the Calculation Office" (Ch. X) and "Bounded apparatus and calculation office" (Ch. XII) arrive without setup; the two-signature rule is never established before it is broken; Ch. XI l.1446, "There had been nine hundred pounds in contributed capital and seven hundred and twenty in customer deposits.", cites capital never raised on the page.
- B4 (Minor). Ch. II-III: the thirty days and the promised written refusal are never closed ("The next afternoon he met Babbage and Lovelace in Dorset Street.").
- B5 (Minor). Ch. III, l.351-358: the failure of the boundaries is stated twice in adjacent paragraphs ("That failed. Every portion pulled upon machinery..." then "each boundary had opened upon something outside it").
- B6 (Minor). Ch. IV, l.486: "The second refusal arrived from Manchester in a wooden box." No first refusal has been named.
- B7 (Minor). Ch. V, l.546: "would be paid to manufacture and was entitled to reject a drawing". Tense and agreement slip.
- B8 (Minor). Ch. VI, l.682: "I won't have him condemn a sound shaft". The "him" is ambiguous; Babbage has not yet entered.
- B9 (Minor). Ch. IX, l.1139-1140: "Halden had advertised for another checker. None could yet challenge a prepared deck". "None" has no antecedent.
- B10 (Note). Ch. IX, l.1068: "which made the theoretical quarter larger". Larger than what is never stated.
- B11 (Note). Ch. IX, l.1168: "For a moment, the old alliance between conditions and limits reappeared." The parties and the sense of "conditions and limits" are unclear.
- B12 (Minor). Ch. X, l.1347-1354: "Guardian's source sheet" in August 1852, when Ch. IX says only "specimen or provisional figures" exist until the signed returns of April 1854.
- B13 (Note). Ch. X, l.1303: "Lovelace began another page with three headings". The page is never named; Ch. XII later refers to "her unanswered succession question".
- B14 (Minor). Ch. XI. "When Halden began to call the third rescue" (l.1470) is garbled; "Before you send another circular" (l.1473) presupposes a circular already sent; l.1393 sends Guardian "the delivery ledger" whole.
- B15 (Minor). Ch. XII, l.1587: "the close hand Henry knew from the Notes". The Notes are printed; a hand is known from letters or manuscripts.
- B16 (Minor). Ch. II, l.176: "Lovelace came to his rooms in Dorset Street". Babbage kept a house there (about 85% sure of the fact; the word suggests lodgings).
- B17 (Note). Ch. VIII, l.889: "nearly seven years" against the book's own dates (a little over seven).
- B18 (Note). Ch. VIII, l.977: "No one remarked upon the change." Explains an image that already works.
- B19 (Minor). Book-wide: mixed American and British spelling ("toward" 12 times beside "towards" 6; "honor", "labor", "favored", "rumor" beside "pencilled", "initialled", "grey"); document typography inconsistent (see 35).
- Shared with V1, same text in V2: A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A8, A10, A11, A12, A13, A14, A16. Not in V2: A7 (V2 gives no April sums, though Ch. I still has Neale mid-check on Lothbury on delivery day), A9 (V2 has no office articles, so "the copy" is unambiguous), A15 (V2 has the summary paragraph but not the phrase).

### Real-world check (both)

I found no factual error before the point of departure. Confident (about 90% or better): Lovelace's Notes and Menabrea's 1842 memoir; the government withdrawal and the earlier Clement dispute; Babbage's house at 1 Dorset Street; Ockham; Whitworth's Manchester works and gauges; the October 1847 credit crisis; Lovelace's death at Great Cumberland Place on 27 November 1852; Charles Babbage's death in 1871 and Henry's army career; Babbage's early work on life assurance. Fairly sure (about 75%): a mid-August 1843 proposal from Ada to Babbage that he resisted, which the chapter reworks. Unsure (about 50%): that Griffith Davies, a real actuary (1788-1855) connected with the Guardian, still held a Guardian post in 1843-54; harmless in an alternate history. Verified by calculation: 7 April 1854 was a Friday, as V1 says. Diction: see A14.

## 4. What still most needs work

In Version 1, most important first.

1. **Give the principal men separate voices and the world some weight.** Babbage, Halden, Davies and Lovelace all speak in the same balanced, epigrammatic register (Halden, an estimator, says "Division makes no one competent. It tells me whose hours enter the price and whose refusal stops the wages."), and nearly every paragraph closes on a compressed line ("Monday had filled itself before it arrived."; "The mechanism's resistance entered Farrow's life first as Friday."). Individually these are the book's best sentences; across twelve thousand words they blur the speakers and make Chapters IV and V (two men and a solicitor arguing clauses) the flattest stretch. Only Margaret, Wills, William and Neale sound like themselves. Let Farrow, his foreman, Davies and Halden speak from their trades; let one negotiation happen with something in hand (Whitworth's gauges opened and used); put smoke, weather, money and food into the rooms (1851, the year of the trial, is the year of the Great Exhibition, and the book never lets it into the room); and thin the closing aphorisms so the best ones land.

2. **Make the fall arithmetically airtight and show its last year.** The tragedy is a sum, so the sums must close. Chapter IX fixes "forty hours per verified packet" and ten hours a week, yet Chapter X has Neale finish Lothbury within the week; say that Lothbury is a small packet, or let Neale work extra hours and let the reader see the cost (A7). Second, 1853 is one summary paragraph ("No single day announced failure; each exception was carried forward"), and "as other exceptions had" promises a pattern the reader has seen only in 1852. One short scene from late 1853, in which a second signature is quietly waived and the office is thanked for it, would make 7 April read as the end of a habit rather than a first lapse, and would let Halden's rationalizations be heard again (in Chapter I they are only recalled). Consider, too, leaving the third direction half a step less on the nose.

3. **Give the lay reader one concrete handle on the technical stakes, and tie off the loose threads.** Nothing on the page shows what a recurrence or a reserve is, or what a transposed first value at age forty-seven does to the entries after it; one worked line in Chapter I or IV would make "small enough to survive an impatient glance and large enough to alter a later reserve" felt rather than asserted, and would explain why Guardian, which hand-computed those ages, still needed the table (A16). Then close the small threads in Section 3: the packet "unopened at one end and cut cleanly along the other" (A1), "Halden's question" never asked on the page (A12), the three origins of the successor register (A3), "Guardian invoked both" (A10), the schedule-authority line (A8), "He held the office pen" (A6), which sheet Henry carries (A13), and the period-wrong "deck" and "protocol" (A14).

Cheap wins from the other version, to keep in V1: "He did not consent or refuse. He recommended that the office wait." (Ch. X), "For several seconds, only the fire answered." (Ch. XII), "The capital page" (Ch. V), and the smoother "after the Notes, after the Turin account had been turned inside out and enlarged" (Ch. II).

2. Halden's 'We gave it' suggests office responsibility. His handwritten authorization to deliver before the second comparison establishes his direct part; he later admits waiving Neale's comparison.

3. Wills transposed and checked against himself; intentional deceit or awareness of the error is not established. Neale was occupied with Lothbury; knowledge of the waiver is unknown. Babbage identifies correct processing of wrong input; bad faith or prior knowledge is not established. Halden authorized the unchecked delivery, then investigates and discloses; knowing the input was wrong at authorization is not established.

4. Friday wages, returnable £180 and another job's deadline pressure Halden. He could request an extension or move Neale and break the other promise. Instead he deferred comparison until Monday, avoiding a difficult letter and preserving appearances with hands for two and four dates.

5. Davies's response, consequences for the people, repayment, jobs, later contracts, the office's survival and changes to checking remain unresolved. Which motives or knowledge would you hesitate to claim?", "What pressures shaped Halden’s delivery decision, and which other choices were available to him?", "What is still uncertain at the end of this opening, including what might happen to the people and office?"], "targetPassage": "## I. The Returned Table\n\nThe packet came back tied with the office's own green tape.\n\nEdward Halden knew the tape because he had ordered twelve dozen yards of it and\nargued down the price. He knew the paper because its weight had been entered in\nthe delivery account. He knew the seal of Guardian Assurance, pressed too hard\ninto the red wax, and Griffith Davies's narrow hand upon the wrapper. What he\ndid not know was why the packet should have returned unopened at one end and\ncut cleanly along the other.\n\nThe calculating room continued behind him. A shaft turned beneath the floor.\nEvery few seconds the card reader lifted, admitted a stiff rectangle, and let\nit fall into the receiving box. The apparatus did not sound like thought. It\nsounded like six metal cupboards being locked in sequence.\n\nDavies's letter contained three sentences.\n\nThe figures in the enclosed table did not agree with Guardian's independent\ncalculation from age forty-seven onward. The office was to suspend the related\nwork. Mr Davies requested the source sheets, the operation cards, both checking\nsignatures, and an account of the discrepancy under clause eleven.\n\nHalden read the letter twice and placed it flat upon his desk. He did not call\nfor Babbage. He did not yet call for the clerk who had prepared the cards. First\nhe opened the returned table.\n\nThe error was not theatrical. No column descended into nonsense. The values\nremained orderly and plausible; each differed from Guardian's by an amount\nsmall enough to survive an impatient glance and large enough to alter a later\nreserve. That was worse. An absurd answer accused itself. A reasonable wrong\nanswer recruited the reader.\n\nHe took the configuration register from the locked cabinet and checked the\nseal. Unbroken. The mechanism described there was still the mechanism in the\nroom: six signed registers, addition and subtraction, the same transfer order,\nthe same limits they had stated three years before. He found the run trace. It\nshowed no jam, correction, or repeated card. The second run agreed with the\nfirst.\n\nBy noon Babbage stood at the long table with his spectacles in one hand and the\nreturned sheets in the other.\n\n“The recurrence is exact,” he said.\n\n“The table is wrong.”\n\n“Wrong, yes, but see where.” Babbage set down his spectacles and ran one finger\nalong the trace. “The first supplied value. After that, every transfer is true.\nNo wheel introduced this. The Engine carried what it was given.”\n\nHalden knew that relief. He had felt it himself on finding the seal unbroken.\nNow Babbage was looking only at the trace.\n\n“We gave it,” Halden said.\n\n“The preparation desk gave it.”\n\n“That desk is in this office.”\n\nBabbage picked up his spectacles. “Then correct the copy and repeat.”\n\nHalden looked through the glass partition. The preparers sat at facing desks,\nreducing customer sheets to a form the cards could carry. Beyond them, the\napparatus continued its patient sequence. To a visitor the machine was the\nmarvel and the clerks were furniture. The accounts said otherwise. For every\nhour of its operation, people spent several hours deciding what it should be\ngiven, and more deciding whether its answer could leave the room.\n\nHe sent for the Guardian source sheet and the preparation copy. At a quarter\npast one, he found the first divergence. Guardian had supplied 3,742. The\npreparation copy read 3,472. The two middle figures had exchanged places in a\nhand so familiar that Halden recognized it before he read the initials.\n\nSamuel Wills came in pale. He had brought the ruler and pencil from his desk\nalthough Halden had asked only for him; he kept them aligned between his hands\nwhile he stood.\n\n“Did you compare this line with the source?” Halden asked.\n\n“I read the copy back, sir.”\n\n“To whom?”\n\nThe young man looked toward the checking room.\n\n“Mr Neale had the Lothbury packet. I read it back to myself.”\n\n“That is not a comparison.”\n\n“No, sir.”\n\n“Who instructed you to release the cards?”\n\nThe clerk said nothing. The ruler shifted in his hands, and he brought its end\nlevel with the pencil again. Halden had been about to ask the question again,\nlouder. He dismissed him instead.\n\nThe young man took both tools away. Through the partition Halden watched him\nlay them square with the edge of his desk before sitting down. Then Halden\nopened the delivery ledger.\n\nThere should have been two marks beside the Guardian job: the preparer's and an\nindependent checker's. There was one. Beneath it, in the margin reserved for an\nexception, was a short authorization in Halden's own hand.\n\nSecond comparison to follow. Delivery permitted to preserve date.\n\nE. H.\n\nHe remembered the morning. The wages had been due on Friday. Guardian's\ndelivery date fell that day; missing it would make its one hundred and eighty\npounds returnable. Neale had been checking another table whose delay would also\nhave cost the office money. Halden had told himself that a single delivery\ncould borrow two days from its own conditions and repay them on Monday.\n\nHe had seen the other choices. He could have asked Davies for an extension and\nadmitted that the office had sold a date it could not safely keep. He could have\nmoved Neale from the Lothbury packet and broken that promise instead. Or he\ncould let one signature stand temporarily for two and preserve both appearances\nuntil Monday. The third course had felt least like a decision because it moved\nno visible object and required no difficult letter. Only a line in the margin\nhad changed.\n\nMonday had filled itself before it arrived.\n\nBabbage read the authorization without sitting down.\n\n“It remains a human failure,” he said. “The apparatus received three thousand\nfour hundred and seventy-two and treated it with perfect fidelity. To charge\nthe mechanism with the table is to confuse obedience to an operation with\njudgment upon its premise.”\n\n“Of course it is.”\n\nThe answer surprised him. Babbage turned.\n\n“Wills transposed two figures,” Halden continued. “I waived Neale's comparison.\nWe sold four dates with hands for two. Which entry do you want first?”\n\n“You have passed from one supplied value to the constitution of the office.\nThat may be a second inquiry; it is not a failure of the calculating\nmechanism.”\n\n“We took one witnessed trial and sold four tables upon it.”\n\nFor a moment neither man spoke. Through the partition came the fall of another\ncard.\n\nOn the shelf above Halden's desk stood the test packet from 1851, its seals cut\nbut preserved. Beside it lay Lady Lovelace's qualification on capacity. He had\nfiled them together because their paper was the same size. Until that morning\nhe had not admitted that they were parts of the same result.\n\nDavies had asked for both checking signatures. Halden dipped his pen and began\nthe reply with the one fact no calculation could improve.\n\nThere was no second signature."}"},"verdict":"Absolute target recovery is 5/5 for each selected passage. {"schema":"meaning-model-story-author-record/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Independent manuscript reader: baseline text only, all twelve chapters read, uninformed of model or proposed changes. Literary diagnosis, not historical verification, blind control comparison or measured improvement.","data":{"review":"# Independent reader report: The Book of Conditions

Read in full: all 11,719 words, extracted only from `story.units[*].text` in array order. No other snapshot fields, theory, source notes, model, or previous reviews consulted. This is a literary diagnosis, not a historical verification.

## Overall reader experience

The book has a real narrative object: a narrow success that cannot by itself make a viable, honest business. The returned packet is an effective opening, and the return from the long retrospective to that packet is intelligible. Physical actions repeatedly make administrative decisions tangible. The book does not need a conventional villain, romance, disaster spectacle, or a different dramatic formula.

Its chief limitation is that the narrator too often explains the meaning of an exchange after the exchange has made it plain. That leaves less interpretive room than the strongest scenes deserve. The central reversal also needs one more piece of practical and emotional causation: Halden knowingly sells twice the available final checking capacity, despite two years in which to train, and subsequently defers the very training used to justify the deposits. This can be credible, but its mechanics are currently asserted more clearly than lived.

## 1. Highest priority: make the broken training promise legible

**Confusing/unearned effect, not merely a preference.** Chapter IX takes care to explain that final customer figures cannot arrive until 1 April 1854, and that Halden has spread preparatory work over two years. His defense of the four deposits is concrete:

> “The deposits keep Wills paid while Neale trains him,” Halden said.

He then promises:

> “We begin training now and accept no fifth.”

In Chapter X, Lovelace proposes training that will cost approximately £120 in the first year, and:

> Halden's answer praised the plan and asked whether it might begin after the four current packets were delivered.

After Babbage's visit, Halden again defers training until the present contracts bring their next payments. I understand the intended distinction between paying a preparer and purchasing genuinely independent competence. The prose has not yet shown sufficiently what happened to the promise to begin, what training actually occurred, or why two available years could not absorb a first-year program. The issue matters because the book's principal practical tragedy turns on it. The opening tells us who waived the final comparison, so the retrospective must earn how this particular man arrives there.

**Action:** establish one precise failed allocation between the deposit decision and the August letters. A concrete collision between Neale's existing hours, the preparation plan, the outside assurance clerk's fee, and a withheld payment would do more than another warning. If informal training starts but cannot yield independent checking, show that distinction. If Halden knowingly spends the training provision elsewhere, let the reader witness that choice and its locally plausible reason. The material already gives enough tools; it does not require an added subplot.

Halden's vanity is a promising motive:

> One letter had called him inventor. He had corrected the word in his reply, but not before reading the salutation twice.

Keep that. It currently has to carry too much of the movement from rigorous estimator to optimistic seller. An additional small instance of enjoying the office he has made would help more than explaining that he has become overconfident.

## 2. High priority: remove second explanations of already effective scenes

**Cumulative loss of interest; the precise amount of cutting is an editorial preference.** Chapters III–VIII repeatedly enact the same compelling disagreement: Babbage broadens the implication, Halden prices the obligation, Lovelace polices the claim. Each version adds an important subject, but the narrator often also states the resulting lesson. The scenes then feel more settled and predictable than their human stakes warrant.

For example, IV has already shown Davies and the works refusing particular terms before it concludes:

> A customer had refused to buy a vision. A works had refused to price unsupported precision.

IX has already dramatized each position and Neale's answer before:

> They stated their choices separately. Babbage chose four and later capacity. Lovelace chose two. Halden chose four and no fifth.

XI gives Margaret a persuasive intervention and then tells us:

> He had spent twelve years teaching other men that a future capacity could not pay a present debt merely because it was described well.

These sentences are individually clean. Together they repeatedly tell the reader what has just been understood. The first chapter similarly spells out all three alternatives after Halden discovers his own waiver; that exposition makes his guilt completely legible but reduces the shock and leaves little to discover later.

**Action:** conduct a cut pass targeted at the paragraph immediately after an effective exchange or action. Keep factual consequences and new contradictions; question thematic restatements. Preserve the deliberate protocol in the test scene where waiting is the experience. Do not simply shorten every technical passage. The book's subject requires technical particulars, but not a verdict after every particular.

## 3. Medium-high priority: allow disagreement to remain human and unresolved more often

**A character-range concern, not a demand that a correct character become wrong.** Lovelace's correspondence is almost unfailingly the best diagnosis; it arrives to settle manufacture, credit, trial, and capacity. Babbage regularly supplies the technically ingenious but institutionally insufficient answer. Halden and Lovelace frequently speak in the same polished adversarial cadence:

> “A machine being paid for must be governed as if somebody can say what is being paid for.”

> “Then we have written sixteen pages to arrive at your memory.”

> “It is a trial of whether we can discover what has been tried.”

I can distinguish their offices more easily than their spontaneous speech. Babbage has the most distinctive recurrent gesture and impatience, but the repeated role of being corrected risks flattening his legitimate claim that a constrained repair may teach less than a redesign. The strong ending of VI acknowledges this properly:

> The machine offered no judgment on the route not taken.

**Action:** preserve the intellectual exchanges but let one or two consequential conversations include a response that is not already an epigram or a completed diagnosis: a particular question, an incomplete answer, a delayed concession, or a practical disagreement left open. The small deputy scene is valuable because Lovelace's insistence has both an intelligible origin and a possible cost. Her exchange with William is better for his not supplying the reassurance she waits for. Retain that ambiguity instead of adding an explicit confession. A little more felt uncertainty elsewhere would let her authority be earned inside scenes rather than arrive fully formed in letters.

## 4. Medium priority: anchor the contract-decision year where it occurs

**Local navigational confusion.** IX moves from the 1851 test to July, December, tables due in 1854, preparatory work spread over two years, and then:

> During March the four preparations began to overlap. In April Lovelace returned to the office decision.

The February decision is mentioned before its year is provided; XI eventually calls it February 1852. A reader without historical dates in memory can momentarily take the March/April passage as 1854, then be pulled backward by Lovelace's illness and death. That is avoidable friction in a book whose chronology supports the argument.

**Action:** attach 1852 to the decision or to the first March transition. One date is sufficient. Do not add a chronology appendix to repair an in-scene problem.

## 5. Medium priority: trust the ending's objects more than its inventory vocabulary

**Primarily a preference about closure, with an observable repetition issue.** The late father-and-son drawing exchange is unusually alive: Charles asks for the next sheet, Henry brings it, and their attention briefly follows the same line. It admits affection and inheritance beyond the office's moral account. Then the inventory conversation restates the governing distinction at length:

> “The distinction was true.” His voice lost its earlier force. “It did not answer the account. The office had undertaken to deliver a correct table.”

The formal second heading lists:

> configuration, proof, qualification, error, correction, and closure, complete.

The 1900 return adds another recapitulation before the tape is tied. I find the final physical act sufficient and moving; the succession of verbal summaries just before it reduces its force.

**Action:** retain the paired headings if their tension matters, but shorten the explanation surrounding them. Test an ending that reaches the wrong table, corrected table, qualification, and faded tape sooner. The complete archive can embody the argument without enumerating every category of it. The 1900 coda is optional: it earns its place through preservation and elapsed time, not new plot information. Keep it brief if retained.

## What to preserve

- The opening's material mystery and moral turn: familiar tape and handwriting lead to Halden recognizing his own authorization. “There was no second signature” is a strong chapter ending.
- The resistant assembly and the foreman's physical check. “He turned it once more after the test was sufficient” admits pleasure without translating it into a lesson.
- The test's slowness, exhausted attention, the three empty strokes after success. This is an earned emotional payoff for a technical book.
- Margaret protecting the working space of her own account, then asking Edward to stay while they untangle the novel's brothers. It gives them a shared life outside the manuscript's central question and does not need more explanation.
- Neale teaching Wills to admit an unreadable figure. The action of leaving it open is stronger than a maxim about uncertainty.
- Lovelace and Babbage's briefly recovered speed at Ockham, interrupted by breath. Their mutual intellectual pleasure gives the loss substance.
- Above all, Wills asking for the delivery order to enter his reference: “Not the copying,” Wills said. “I did that.” / “Only the other part as well.” This is the book's clearest meeting of procedure, unequal power, fear, and self-respect. Do not polish the hesitation out of it.
- The refusal to pretend Babbage's unbuilt alternative has been disproved, and the refusal to let closure become an uncomplicated victory. Halden's final “It does” is better than a self-exonerating speech.

## Boundaries of this diagnosis

I did not fact-check the historical counterfactual. The story reads as deliberately constructed alternate history; any publication need for a framing note depends on material outside the permitted manuscript and is not a finding here. I am not asking for greater spectacle or additional suffering. The needed work is chiefly to clarify the practical hinge and leave more room around the excellent actions already on the page.

{"schema":"meaning-model-review/v1","kind":"review","text":"# Independent comparison: The Book of Conditions

This is a **labeled before/after comparison, not a blind reading**. I read the complete `book/baseline.md` (11,719 words) followed by the complete `book/candidate-v1.md` (11,677 words), then inspected their diff to locate changes. I did not consult other reviews, model records, or agent notes. References below use candidate line numbers unless otherwise specified. This is a literary assessment, not a historical or technical fact check.

## Overall judgment

**Prefer the candidate after two localized repairs.** It is a modest, real improvement, principally in scene causality and the final father–son exchange. Most of the prose, and most of its strengths, are inherited unchanged. It does not substantially reinvent or differentiate the voices. Its best edits remove a second explanation after a scene has already made its point; its best addition lets a character cause a failure that the baseline largely summarized.

The substantial new scene in IX earns its space. The replacement in XI, immediately before the closure resolution, does not: it removes useful mixed motives and introduces an unclear accounting gesture at the moment a consequential decision needs to be legible. Chapter X also needs two short continuity adjustments because training is now explicitly underway.

Confidence is high in those local judgments and moderate in the overall preference. The candidate was read second, so recognition may make its shortened passages feel more sufficient than they would to a new reader. It is therefore significant that the knowledge supporting most cuts is also present earlier within the candidate itself. I would not describe this as a large improvement in overall literary quality.

## Keep

1. **IX: the interrupted lesson (1207–1226).** This is the clearest improvement. Halden has promised, “We begin training now,” and the candidate lets him keep the promise in form while defeating it in practice:

   > “The cards first, Wills. Then come back.”

   > By the time the cards were ready, Neale's paid hours for that day were over.

   The causal sequence is comprehensible without an explanatory speech: urgent production consumes the hours intended to create future capacity. “Another preparer would have to learn the arrangement” gives Halden a plausible local reason, so the scene is more than a demonstration that he is wrong. His familiar ruler and pencil leave with Wills; Neale leaves the specimen in place. Those separate actions make the interrupted relationship tangible.

   Keep “He did not cancel it.” Its position after the completed card order lets the sentence register as Halden's defense of himself. It adds ambiguity about his self-understanding without concealing what he did. The passage makes the later delivery exception an escalation of an observed habit, rather than only the consequence of an abstract capacity calculation.

2. **XII: the shorter Babbage concession (1607–1617).** Prefer:

   > “The distinction was true.”

   > Henry waited.

   > “But they bought the table,” Charles said.

   The baseline recapitulates the machine/office distinction twice, including “The office had undertaken to deliver a correct table.” The candidate keeps Babbage's need to defend the truth of his distinction, then makes his concession an effort he reaches after Henry waits. The plain final sentence works because it is a departure from his habitual argumentative precision. The surrounding drawing exchange and “Of that object … Not of the Engine” preserve his resistance; this is not a conversion speech. Removing his explicit tribute to Lovelace here loses a little overt recognition, but her surviving qualification and the last physical arrangement of the papers carry her importance without reinstating the recap.

3. **VI: Lovelace's response to the failed assembly (712–716).** The candidate asks:

   > Could Farrow state a new tolerance for the shared drive and inspect it?

   and admits:

   > She could not tell from the report whether Babbage's design would prove the better machine.

   This is more convincingly a practical answer from an absent person than the baseline's lesson about parts satisfying “local conditions” and failing “in composition.” The conditional question establishes what can be tried while preserving uncertainty over which design is superior. It also keeps Lovelace from becoming the narrator's infallible mouthpiece. “Neither proposal had yet turned the handle” belongs to this narrator's material vocabulary and leads naturally to Halden's unsuccessful attempt to move it. Preserve the later recognition that Babbage's untried improvement might still be better.

4. **IX: the date and agency of the capacity entry (1065–1066).** “In February 1852, Halden entered eighty hours” provides an unobtrusive temporal anchor before the 1854 delivery schedule, and identifies the estimate as his undertaking. The baseline postpones naming the decision's year until much later. The date improves orientation without inserting an explanatory digression.

5. **IX: compressing the decision summary (1199–1205).** “Neither could sign a customer's acceptance for Halden” and the four dated acceptances are enough to place responsibility. The baseline's explicit three-way ballot and restatement of all authorities make the scene stop to pronounce its own result. The candidate preserves the voices already heard in debate and then moves into the hand signing the papers. Lovelace's request to record her objection is useful action, not merely a narrated category of dissent.

6. **IV: the shorter ending (517–518).** Keep the cut of “A customer had refused to buy a vision. A works had refused to price unsupported precision.” Both refusals have already been enacted. The total at the end is still characteristic of Halden and the narrator. The cut gives the chapter a cleaner exit; it does not need a replacement moral.

7. **V: the shortened authority paragraph (578–580).** Keep the concrete limits of her signature and the household constraint. The removed “one bounded consequence to an authority that the surrounding world did not give her generally” restates what the surrounding social and contractual details let us see. Crucially, keep the entire deputy scene preceding this paragraph: “Chosen by whom?” and her striking out the provision make her later admission to William complicated and earned.

8. **XII: the shortened final inventory (1683–1685).** Slight preference for the candidate. “Side by side” already supplies the equality that “equally preserved” explains. The seal and its date are not needed for orientation at this point. The repeated widening handwriting and the final act of tying remain, preserving both emotional and material continuity. This is a small gain, not a reason by itself to prefer a version.

## Revise before acceptance

**X: complete the training distinction (1290–1301 and 1360–1361).** Keep the added distinction between learning “between preparations” and protected time away from preparation. It makes Lovelace's proposal concrete and explains why the proposed expenditure is additional. But the unchanged sentence:

> Neither paper gave her a day on which Wills would begin.

now momentarily contradicts the immediately preceding statement that he “still learned from Neale,” as well as the new March scene. Likewise, “deferring training until the present contracts produced their next payments” can sound as though all training has been suspended, although the candidate has carefully established something more specific.

Change only the referents: the missing date should be the date Wills would be released from preparation for the proposed instruction; the deferred commitment should be that allocation of paid time. There is no need to explain the whole distinction again. The new scene supplies the explanation. This is a high-confidence continuity repair, not a request for another scene.

## Reject this replacement; preserve the useful motive

**XI: the new paragraph before the closure resolution (1476–1477).** The candidate substitutes:

> New money might keep Wills and Neale employed. Halden left room for it in the account, below the sums Margaret had asked him to pay first.

for the baseline's temptation, which includes “preserve Halden's standing” and the risk of presenting a disclosed failure as proof that the system has already corrected itself.

“Left room for it” is too indeterminate here. Is he budgeting on another subscription, keeping open the option of reopening, or merely leaving blank space? The next sentence is “He wrote the closure resolution.” That jump obscures the decision rather than leaving a productive uncertainty about the man. The account is described immediately above as unable to sustain the remaining work; the new gesture does not tell us what has resolved his temptation to raise more capital.

The cut also gives his temptation only the benevolent motive of keeping Wills and Neale employed. The lost interest in preserving his own standing matters: Halden can do the responsible thing while still wishing to save his reputation. This is consistent with his earlier pleasure at being called an inventor and with Wills having to prompt a fuller reference after the supposedly complete closure account.

Do not necessarily restore all five baseline lines. Its last sentence, about having spent twelve years teaching others, is an explicit moral summation and can go. **Retain the mixed motive and a legible refusal of the proposed circular; reject the ambiguous “left room for it” action.** The immediately preceding imagined circular and Margaret's question already carry much of the reasoning. A shorter paragraph can preserve “New money might preserve Halden's standing and keep Wills and Neale employed” without giving up the candidate's restraint.

## Distinctive voices and passages to protect

The narrator has a recognizable intelligence: dry wit, exact institutional detail, and the tendency to locate an abstraction in an object or a paid hour. “The mechanism's resistance entered Farrow's life first as Friday” and “Monday had filled itself before it arrived” belong to that voice. Do not strip all judgments or aphorisms merely because some of the candidate's deletions work. The revisions succeed where an immediately preceding scene has already supplied the insight.

Babbage remains expansive, defensive about the exact extent of a finding, and unable to leave a drawing alone. Halden speaks in wages, dates, and quantities, but borrows Babbage's confidence when it suits him. Lovelace answers with sharply bounded questions and can be possessive about the authority she has won. Those distinctions survive the candidate; they are not newly created by it. Their shared tendency to deliver polished antitheses is still noticeable, so I would not claim that this pass has solved all voice convergence. Additional ornamental verbal quirks would not help.

The smaller voices are often the most individually persuasive. Preserve Margaret's “Let me finish this line,” the subsequent muddle over the two brothers in her novel, and William's choice to ask whether the water is cool instead of endorsing Ada's self-justification. They give these people attention and desires outside the venture's argument. Preserve Davies's “Before or after I pay?” and Neale's “Nor can I … Leave it open.” Their economy distinguishes them from the principal debaters.

Above all, retain Wills's reference scene unchanged. “Not the copying … I did that” and “Only the other part as well” make him neither an abstract victim nor a mouthpiece for institutional responsibility. Halden taking a fresh sheet instead of writing small is earned by the pressure between them. The candidate wisely leaves this alone. Also preserve the three purposeless strokes after the successful test and the shared drawing at Ockham: these moments let delight coexist with the errors the narrative investigates.

The candidate's strongest change therefore concerns **how the failure happens**, with a smaller improvement to how Babbage can acknowledge it. Its chief risk is treating explicitness as inherently undesirable: the XI replacement demonstrates that a material gesture can still be less clear and less psychologically rich than a short statement of competing motives.
